The Reefs of EarthR. A. Lafferty

⌕
§
About the Novel

The Reefs of Earth (Berkley Medallion, 1968) follows the Dulanty family, Puca (alien fairy-folk) who have been living on Earth for ten years. When tragedy strikes, the six surviving children (or seven, if you count Bad John) decide upon a simple solution to their problems: kill everyone else on Earth.

What follows is a comic fairy tale set in Lost Haven, Oklahoma, blending Irish folklore, Catholic theology, frontier violence, and Lafferty's linguistic exuberance.

About This Guide

This companion follows all sixteen chapters and gives character profiles, a gazetteer, Puca lore, and thematic readings. Quotations and factual references use the printed pages of the Berkley Medallion edition (March 1968). Use the sidebar or the full-text search to explore the guide. See Sources & Editorial Notes.

❧
The 1968 Novel

The Berkley Medallion edition appeared in March 1968. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction identifies it as Lafferty’s first-completed novel; Past Master, The Reefs of Earth, and Space Chantey all appeared within a few months of one another. Composition order and publication order differ.

Sources: John Clute, “Lafferty, R A,” The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction.

The Chapter Poem

Lafferty structures the novel's sixteen chapter titles as a single Bagarthach-style poem, a prophecy of violence and transformation.

To Slay the Folks and Cleanse the Land And Leave the World a Reeking Roastie High Purpose of the Gallant Band And Six Were Kids, and One a Ghostie.
A Child's a Monster Still Uncurled The World's a Trap, and None Can Quit It— The "Strife Dulanty" With the World Was Mostly That They Didn't Fit It.
No Setting For the Gallant Brood In Sacred Groves of Yew or Lindens They Found a Hold More Near Their Blood A Mountainful of Murdered Indians
In Brazen Clash of Helm and Greave Fit Subject For Heroic Chantey The Battle Joined That Could But Leave Or Altered World or Dead Dulanty.

Analysis

The sixteen titles can be read as a Bagarthach-like prophecy. They move from the children’s murderous purpose through their difficulty fitting Earth and their affinity with the dead to a battle whose announced alternatives are an altered world or a dead Dulanty.

Structural Notes

The poem consists of four ABAB quatrains: Land/Band and Roastie/Ghostie, for example, form the first alternating set. Its last two lines do not form a rhyming couplet. The closing line names the two possible outcomes.

The Heroic Chantey

Chapter 14's title, "Fit Subject For Heroic Chantey," promises that Henry's death will be commemorated in song. The chapter delivers, with Latin and English verse fragments appearing as section headers, culminating in the epitaph: "Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum" ("Nothing about monsters except good").

Click any line above to navigate to that chapter.

❧
Meter and Movement

The contents-page titles use four ABAB quatrains with a predominantly iambic four-beat movement. The second and fourth lines of each stanza have feminine endings: roastie/ghostie, quit it/fit it, lindens/Indians, chantey/Dulanty. The movement is jaunty, like a nursery rhyme. The Heroic Chantey later shifts toward a falling rhythm; the two poems differ in meter.

Synopsis

The children’s campaign and the adults’ persecution cross through an axe, a set of hired captors, and a final hunt. All page references are to the 1968 Berkley text.

Two Families in Lost Haven

Henry and Witchy Dulanty are parents of Elizabeth, Charles, and Helen. Frank and Veronica are parents of Peter, Dorothy, John, and the already dead Bad John. The two brothers married two sisters. Sent to Earth more than ten years earlier, the adults have failed to establish accord with its people. Their six-week residence in Lost Haven ends in catastrophe.

[1968, pp. 12–23]

The children’s customary ghost stories open the book. Chapter 2 then gives the family’s arrival and decline: Helen curses Crocker, Peter curses Stutgard, and the adults suffer Earth Allergy. Veronica dies two days before Henry’s arrest. Witchy is confined, and Frank’s grief and drinking give way to an illness that can resemble drunkenness even when he is sober.

[1968, pp. 15–23, 33, 58]

The Axe and the Raft

The children decide to kill everyone else, though Elizabeth and Charles initially favour a shorter list. Their attempt to burn the adults with a Bagarthach is countered. John reaches Stutgard’s room to murder him and finds Crocker has already done it. John takes Crocker’s bloody axe; Elizabeth later hides it. Henry is arrested for the murder.

[1968, pp. 24–35]

From Fulbert, held in the flimsy Lost Haven jail, the children obtain the Île de France. They attack the Stinkers, Stutgard Landing, and Fiddler’s Landing, then encounter Phoebe Jane’s hospitality and raid the Fabers. Gunfire, attempted drownings, and arson make their intent real, though their targets escape.

[1968, pp. 35–56]

Parallel Struggles

Frank evades a lynch mob and humiliates Crocker with its noose. Witchy recites her Devil verses in the institution at Vinita. The children find a home among the dead of Misu Mound, where the history of the burials is disputed; Peter suffers a disturbing passion of Earth Sickness. Henry’s confession overwhelms an old priest, whose death a month later is attributed to it by the narrator.

[1968, pp. 57–74]

Crocker hires Baxter Bushyhead, Little Sad Sam Jones, and Harold Harvestman to capture the children. Charles marches them into the woods and returns with ears. The narrator’s confirmation of a silencer, together with Dorothy’s later completed accusation, is strong evidence of killings offstage. Pandemonium John brings news from the parents and leads a great concert, mixing delight, cruelty, and musical invention.

[1968, pp. 75–90, 106]

Marshall’s interview with Henry exposes both racial hatred and the fraud supporting Lost Haven: bogus relief checks and crop claims, with Marshall expecting to inherit Stutgard’s business. The lawyer’s visit brings out the axe evidence, but Henry mistakes approaching help for danger and escapes at 8:55 p.m. in Chapter 12. Marshall turns the escape into a murderous public spectacle.

[1968, pp. 91–114]

The Hunt and the Bog

John Loose Screw and Sammy Bluefield help Henry. After a roadblock and crash, Henry reaches Thomas Butterfield’s farm. Butterfield phones the authorities despite Henry’s warnings. Marshall shoots Henry in the shoulder from behind, then in the groin and gut; Crocker fires the fatal shot into his face. Marshall kills Butterfield to remove the witness.

[1968, pp. 115–128]

Crocker hunts Bad John through the bogs as his dogs desert him in groups. Frank catches him with the noose. Frank intends afterward to urge the children toward gentleness, but Marshall strikes him from behind before he can speak to them. The rope slips and Crocker sinks. Marshall rolls Frank into the bog. Charles runs up firing; Phoebe Jane’s hidden shot kills Marshall. Charles believes he did it and rolls Marshall’s body in.

[1968, pp. 129–138]

Names and Departure

That afternoon the children intuit their Puca names. Bad John has already been absent for hours. After they cast off, Witchy joins them through Phoebe’s aid and explains that Bad John has gone with Frank. Witchy revises the extermination plan toward control and alteration, still permitting killing and losing her thought about responsibility. She releases the Dragons’ Seed, continues through her last joke about dying, and receives Elizabeth’s answer. Six young pairs of eyes shine beside the older pair fading in death.

[1968, pp. 139–144]
Six little pair of goblin eyes glowing green in the dark; and a seventh older pair nictitated by death slumber to a fainter green. And opposed to them, only the defenseless World!
— Narrator [1968, p. 144]

Chapter 1

To Slay the Folks and Cleanse the Land

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 7–14]

The Dulanty children tell ghost stories in the Big Shanty, exorcising the bleakness of Earth through whistling in the dark.

Summary

The novel opens with an introduction to the Dulanty family: Puca aliens living in the Big Shanty in Lost Haven, Oklahoma. The six children (or seven, if you count Bad John) gather at night to tell ghost stories, their way of defying the "meanest world in all the universes."

The six tales vary in their dealings with death. Elizabeth’s concerns Albert and his unnamed wife, whose verse releases a murderous dog from a picture. Charles tells of a hotel man found dead; Helen of the still-whittling Silly Jimmy; Peter of Alice, Clarissa, and the guard from Hell; Dorothy of a train passing through the shanty; and John of William’s terrible return to Polly. [1968, pp. 7–14]

Bad John, the ghost child, cannot participate in the ritual: "he could only tell people stories, and nobody cares about them." He has no bed in the loft where the other children sleep. When the lights go out, nobody knows where he goes. He "couldn't whistle" in the dark.

Key Events

  • Introduction of all seven children and their relationships
  • Establishment of the Aorach story form
  • First description of the Puca appearance (goblin vs. human-looking)
  • Introduction of the green glowing eyes motif
  • Establishment of Bad John's nature as a ghost child

Characters Introduced

Elizabeth (9) Charles (8) Peter (8) Helen (6) Dorothy (7) John (6) Bad John (ghost)

Aorach Stories Told

§
Elizabeth's Story: The Haunted Picture

A Puca couple buys a picture of a man. The wife notices the eyes change from green to brown, the hair from red to black. Then she notices a dog in the picture that wasn't there before. She makes a careless Bagarthach verse hoping the dog bites her husband, and it does, killing him.

Bagarthach Verse (within story)
I'm turning livid in this bog,
This woolly world that spooks and spites you.
You'll find that picture's got a dog!
I hope the blinking bugger bites you!
— The wife in Elizabeth's story[1968, p. 8]

Moral: "Earth things are so dumb that they don't know when to obey a Bagarthach and when not to."

§
Charles's Story: The Country Hotel

Charles’s traveling salesman finds a terrifying instability of identities at a country hotel. The tale identifies the corpse as the hotel man, with his throat cut. The building vanishes, and the doorknob the traveler carries becomes a rock. [1968, pp. 9–10]

§
Helen's Story: Silly Jimmy

A man returns to his hometown and talks to Silly Jimmy by the railroad tracks. His family reminds him that Silly Jimmy died long ago, run over by a train. Yet fresh wood shavings prove Jimmy had been whittling, dead or not.

Bagarthach Verse (within story)
The engine spattered him like tar,
And broke his bones and burst his belly.
We gathered Jimmy in a jar.
Hey, pass the Silly Jimmy Jelly!
— Made about Silly Jimmy's death[1968, p. 11]
§
Peter's Story: Alice and Clarissa

Alice was sent to Hell for Clarissa’s theft. Returning to frighten her sister, she loses her ghost sheet to Clarissa. The guard mistakes Clarissa for Alice and carries Clarissa away; Alice stays on Earth. [1968, pp. 11–12]

§
Dorothy's Story: The Ghost Train

Dorothy tells of the dead lantern-bearer and the train that killed him. The train takes the old track beneath the shanty. She says she made a sign: it passed through without breaking the house up. [1968, p. 13]

§
John's Story: William and Polly

A Puca boy named William marries an Earth girl named Polly. They promise that whoever dies first will return to tell the other what death is like. William dies; Polly remarries a man named Tom. On their wedding night, someone comes to the door three times. Tom relays the messages: "He said to tell you that it sure is cold." Polly says it must be the coal man. "He said to tell you that it sure is dark." The kerosene man. "He said to tell you that it sure is lonesome." Polly tells Tom to send him away: "I don't care any more how it is there."

A great wind kills Tom, freezes Polly stiff, blows away the house, opens a hole, and buries Polly. William’s messages tell Polly what death is like: cold, dark, lonesome. [1968, pp. 13–14]

Puca Lore Introduced

  • Aorach: a Puca story art, including these ghost tales but also Veronica’s story of the sisters’ births. [1968, pp. 7–14, 18–19]
  • Bagarthach verse: Rhymed verses with magical power; Earth things "are so dumb that they don't know when to obey a Bagarthach and when not to"
  • Puca appearance: Some look human, others are "potato-faced goblins, like real Pucas." Elizabeth, Charles, and Helen can pass as Earth children; Peter, Dorothy, John, and Bad John have the true goblin look. Witchy "said that they had planned it that way, that some of the children should look like children of this place, and some of them should look like the children back home."
  • Green eyes: "Look at them straight, and you'd hardly notice a thing. But look at them sideways... they'd scare the liver out of you." Eyes that "glowed like green coals."

Notable Quotations

"Listen, people, creatures, devices, entities, it was the meanest world in all the universes! It'd have spooked you too."
[1968, p. 7]
We don’t know why anyone would want to visit it. We sure don’t know why anyone would want to be born on it. But the children hadn’t been able to control their place of birth.
— Narrator [1968, p. 7]
"It was their way of defying that tricky place Earth. That place will hurt you if you let it get the hop on you. They spooked the Earth spooks away with their stories. They whistled in the dark."
[1968, p. 14]
❧
The Irish Words Behind the Arts

The Puca name recalls Irish púca, a fairy or goblin; Peter’s Ifreann is the Irish word for hell. The threatening verse belongs to a wider tradition of dangerous Irish rhymers: Rosalind’s joke about having been an Irish rat in As You Like It 3.2 presupposes the belief that rats could be rhymed to death. Rosalind’s joke is a literary parallel for the Bagarthach. [1968, pp. 7–14]

Sources: Shakespeare, As You Like It 3.2.

Chapter 2

And Leave the World a Reeking Roastie

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 15–23]

The Dulantys arrive in Lost Haven, where hostility greets them, and Helen kills a man with a verse before he knows he's dead.

Summary

This chapter provides the backstory: how the Dulanty families came to Lost Haven six weeks before the main action. They traveled in two station wagons and two trucks: Veronica drove one wagon with all the children, Witchy drove the other "loaded with everything in the world," Henry drove the sideboard truck with the furniture, and Frank drove the van carrying "the tools and shops of the several professions of the two brothers."

They stopped for lunch in what appeared to be a weed patch. A hostile man appeared, barking at them: "We won't have our town dirtied up by strangers. You're the strangest clutch I ever saw." Henry demanded: "Where's any town?" The man replied: "You're standing in the middle of Lost Haven", the town so overgrown it was invisible. This was Crocker. Helen killed him with a Bagarthach verse, though it would take weeks for him to realize he was dead.

Half an hour later, a bigger man arrived: Coalfactor Stutgard, owner of the town. "I don't know what you are," he said, "but you don't belong anywhere on God's green Earth." Peter whispered to the children, "Let me kill this one," and growled his own killing verse. A furtive local then told them Stutgard lied: one house wasn't his: the Big Shanty, owned by an Indian lady in Catoosa.

The chapter also reveals the Puca mission: sent to Earth as "picked young couples" to achieve accord with humanity, or failing that, to "do something about the planet." Ten years in, they have achieved neither.

Veronica, "the real center of the two families," mother to some children and aunt to the rest, dies suddenly of Earth Allergy. Frank takes her death "all wrong," his merriment at the wake forced, his Bagarthach verses falling short. Watching their children play, Henry observes: "They can't really adapt to Earth, I see it now. The question then becomes: Can the Earth adapt to them?" The chapter ends with Henry raising his head, listening "as to the sounding of a horn off Earth."

Key Events

  • Arrival in Lost Haven six weeks prior
  • First confrontation with Crocker → Helen's killing verse
  • Confrontation with Coalfactor Stutgard → Peter's killing verse
  • Move into the Big Shanty (owned by an Indian lady in Catoosa)
  • Background on the Puca mission to Earth
  • Veronica's death from Earth Allergy
  • Witchy's descent into madness
  • Frank begins drinking heavily
  • Children sing a crow down from the sky to eat

Characters Introduced

Henry Dulanty Frank Dulanty Veronica Witchy Crocker Coalfactor Stutgard

Bagarthach Verses

Helen's Curse on Crocker
Old Crocker man, be belled and banged!
You hound-dog hunk, we'll have you hounded!
On else than gallows be you hanged!
In else than water be you drownded!
— Helen, Chapter 2 ☠ Delayed Kill[1968, p. 15]
Peter's Curse on Stutgard
Too long, too late you steal and strut;
Your bubble breaks, your grip relaxes!
Beware the under-studding, Stut!
Beware of jackals bearing axes!
— Peter, Chapter 2 ☠ Delayed Kill[1968, p. 16]

"It's funny that when you kill a man, he's often the last one to know about it."

Helen's Crow-Summoning Verse
I catch you, crow, in curving orb
No matter how you caw and cough you!
I sing the corbie to the corb!
I sing the silly wings right off you!
— Helen, summoning food[1968, p. 23]

Elizabeth calls to Helen: "Sing us a bird!... A big one with black juice in it!" Helen enters "a sly ecstasy" and sings the verse. A crow jerks down from the sky "as though caught in a wire loop." Charles and Peter catch it at their fingertips and tear it apart, "gulping the black-red blood that tasted of hot salt and iron." They prefer crow to "white-meat barnyard peckers."

Puca Lore

  • Earth Allergy: Fatal to adult Puca; attacks liver and kidneys (seat of good humor); taints one with the "Earth outlook"
  • The mission: achieve accord with Earth and consider whether something could be done with the planet. [1968, p. 20]
  • The Four Worlds: Earth belongs to a group the novel does not fully identify; Mercator, Astrobe, and Camiroi appear elsewhere. [1968, pp. 20–21, 73]
  • Indian Affinity: Puca were told they'd be "in rapport with the Indian population" but found them a "vanishing minority"; their information was "centuries out of date"
  • The Hive Ghost: Frank’s account of humanity’s alarming communal instinct. His claim that Earth people act without thinking is a Puca judgment. [1968, p. 21]

Deaths

Two days before Henry’s arrest
Veronica ☠ Earth Allergy
"I can't very die just yet. Witchy is going out of her wits and she needs me. If I die, the family will break up." She was the "real center" of the two families: mother of some children, aunt to the rest. "No creature of any species could dislike her. That was not true of the rest of them."

The Aorach of Veronica's Conception

Veronica tells her characteristic Aorach story explaining how she and Witchy were "twins" born eleven months apart, conceived the same night but by separate acts, when their mother briefly went to bed at one minute before 4 a.m. (when Papa had to light the furnace at the brickyard). "An Earth doctor... told Veronica that such a thing was impossible... Imagine an Earth doctor trying to tell a mistress of the Aorach about something as fundamental as that."

Notable Quotations

"They remind me of the fireflies on Mercator. You remember how the millions of those pseudoinsects would cluster on hillocks and trees and all pulsate with their light together? Those on one hill would answer the beacon flashes of those on another hill, and yet they were creatures so small that fifty of them could be heaped on the end of your finger—and blind."
— Frank Dulanty, on Earth people
[1968, p. 21]
"The Hive Ghost hovers over them invisible, and they feel it from one end of their communities to the other. We can handle Earth individuals as though they were furniture or stones, but we cannot handle the Hive Ghost that hangs over them. And it hates us, Henry."
— Frank Dulanty
[1968, p. 21]
"They can't really adapt to Earth, I see it now. The question then becomes: Can the Earth adapt to them?"
— Henry Dulanty
[1968, p. 23]
❧
Pilgrims and Predicted Deaths

The opening “pilgrims on Earth” recalls Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11, where human life is understood as a pilgrimage. The Dulantys give that language an extraterrestrial sense. Peter’s “jackals bearing axes” adapts the warning about Greeks bearing gifts associated with Virgil’s Laocoon. Crocker and his axe will make the adapted warning literal. Helen’s “be belled” recalls Aesop’s mice and their plan to bell the cat; Frank later brings the noose. [1968, pp. 15–16, 31–32, 63]

Sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2.49; Aesop, “Belling the Cat”.

Chapter 3

High Purpose of the Gallant Band

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 24–32]

The children conceive their great plan: kill everyone in the world except the six of them (or seven, if you count Bad John).

Summary

The chapter opens with the children's logical conclusion: "If there were only six persons in the world (or seven, if you count Bad John), the Earth would be a much better place." Their plan is simple: kill everyone. Elizabeth dissents, willing to kill only specific targets: "the first man to bark at them" (Crocker), Mrs. Cowper with "eyes like a little pig," Mr. Cranker with "hairs in his ears." Charles adds the Bacons, Lanyards, Kirbys, Fabers, plus Elwood Elgin, Rex Remagen, Barney Bottleby, and Sheriff Train, but thinks "that was almost enough." Helen overrules them: "The whole thing becomes silly unless you kill everybody." She hints that Elizabeth, at nine, might be "borderline" herself.

Dorothy sings a Bagarthach verse to burn down the Big Shanty with the adults inside. The children spend the afternoon swimming: Elizabeth the strongest swimmer, Helen the fastest and slipperiest, Charles diving from the very tops of the tall sycamores. While drying on branches, four tell parabolic stories about recent traumas: Elizabeth's of finding Witchy mad; Peter's of Frank's drinking; John's of burying Veronica; Helen's prophetic dream of her father in jail.

That night John draws the task of killing Stutgard. Bad John goes ahead but is a poor lookout because darkness means nothing to him. He reports that another man has already killed Stutgard. Peter resents this intrusion upon the children’s intended victims, and they proceed to the house. [1968, pp. 30–31]

They proceed anyway, forming a human tower: Peter on Elizabeth's shoulders, Helen on Peter's, Dorothy on Helen's, Charles on Dorothy's. John climbs the swaying tower with his small axe "as sharp as a corn knife." But when he emerges, he carries a different axe: larger, heavier, a man's axe, bloody. Helen insists he killed Stutgard: "People who don't love blood don't love anything." But John admits Bad John was right. The Bagarthach to burn the shanty also fails. They return home confused, leave the bloody axe on the back porch, and go to bed under the same roof as Henry and Frank, their next intended victims.

Key Events

  • Decision to kill everyone in the world (Helen overrules Elizabeth and Charles's partial genocide)
  • Dorothy's Bagarthach to burn the Big Shanty (fails; countered by adults)
  • Swimming shows extraordinary speed and endurance underwater, with limits made explicit in Peter’s later distress. [1968, pp. 26, 69–70]
  • Four parabolic stories told while drying on sycamore branches
  • Night mission: human tower formed to reach Stutgard's window
  • Bad John reports Stutgard already dead; children proceed anyway
  • John finds Stutgard murdered, retrieves Crocker's bloody axe
  • Big Shanty did not burn; the verse failed against the Kindred
  • Children leave axe on porch, sleep under same roof as their next targets

Characters Mentioned

Mrs. Stutgard (target) Mrs. Cowper ("pig eyes") Mr. Cranker ("hairy ears") Elwood Elgin Rex Remagen Barney Bottleby Sheriff Train

Bagarthach Verses

Dorothy's Verse to Kill the Adults (FAILED)
We'll wither Witchy with a prank,
And kindle them in flames like roses—
Veronica and Hank and Frank—
And give them all Apotheosis.
— Dorothy, Chapter 3 (countered by adults' Bagarthach)[1968, p. 24]

Frank explains the failure by the adults’ counterverse and says the spell cannot be used against Kindred. Elizabeth’s earlier tale also has a Puca husband dying through a verse. Dorothy has also included the already dead Veronica. [1968, pp. 8–9, 24, 35]

Helen's Dream-Verse (ineffective)
I blast you corny country cops,
I'll blow the bars and locks, by hokey!
I'll kill the sheriff's cows and crops,
And get my papa out of pokey.
— Helen, in her prophetic story (within a dream, doesn't work)[1968, p. 30]

The Parabolic Stories

§
Elizabeth's Story: The Floozy

A thinly veiled account of finding Witchy gone mad the night before. A little girl follows her mother's perfume through dark streets and finds "a crazy floozy." The floozy turns and says "My God, Elizabeth! That you should see me like this." The girl runs home and looks in a mirror: "It wasn't her at all... It had all happened to somebody else and to somebody else's mother."

§
Peter's Story: The Brown Bottle

A boy watches his father drink from a brown bottle. With each glass, the father changes: "like the man in the story that changed into a frog." His eyes go gray and glazed, his face reddens, his arms darken. "The little boy is afraid to see if his own father has come back yet today." (An account of Frank's drinking.)

§
John's Story: The Onion and the Crate

A boy and his mother have only one onion to eat, eating one layer each night. When it's gone, the mother dies. The boy brings another onion, but she's been put in a crate. Her cold-iron grip catches his hand and won't let go. The men say they'll saw his arm off. "Get in or get out," they tell him. Unable to decide, they push him into the crate and bury him with his mother. (An account of Veronica's death and burial.)

§
Helen's Story: Papa in Jail

Helen tells of a girl visiting her father in jail and trying to free him with a verse. She says Bagarthach often fails in a dream. The story anticipates Henry’s imprisonment and the children’s departure. [1968, pp. 29–30]

Deaths

Night of Chapter 3
Coalfactor Stutgard ☠ Axe Murder
Found dead by John when the children arrive to kill him. Killed by Crocker with his own axe, witnessed by Bad John, who "could be outside the cellar, and then inside again, or into the Stutgards' house and in all the rooms of it, and out again without using the doors." Peter's earlier Bagarthach fulfilled: "Beware of jackals bearing axes!"

Puca Lore

  • Kindred: Frank attributes the failure to a successful counterverse. [1968, p. 35]
  • Bad John's nature: Can pass through walls, unlatch windows from inside, be in multiple places, but "didn't know what it meant to be dark"
  • Swimming: the children stay below the surface far longer than humans. Peter nevertheless reaches the limit of even Puca lungs in Chapter 8. [1968, pp. 26, 69–70]
  • Love of blood: "People who don't love blood don't love anything"; the Puca have no squeamishness about violence

Notable Quotations

If there were only six persons in the world (or seven, if you count Bad John), the Earth would be a much better place. All you had to do was kill all the other people on Earth.
— Narrator, entering the children’s reasoning [1968, p. 24]
"The whole thing becomes silly unless you kill everybody."
— Helen, overruling Elizabeth's partial genocide
[1968, p. 25]
"I'm almost four foot tall and as salty a man or boy as there is on Earth. I can kill anybody I want to."
— John, age 6
[1968, p. 31]
"Nobody better be poaching on our preserve."
— Peter, on learning Stutgard was already murdered
[1968, p. 31]
"People who don't love blood don't love anything."
— Helen
[1968, p. 32]
"Just imagine a man killing another man, and neither of them a Puca. It almost makes me sick."
— Elizabeth
[1968, p. 32]
❧
A Grand Name for Killing

Dorothy’s Apotheosis means elevation to divine status. Her verse makes the destruction of the parents sound like their glorification. The narrator’s avunculi means maternal uncles. Helen’s corbie is a Scots word for a crow or raven. [1968, pp. 24–26]

← Chapter 2 · Chapter 4 →

Chapter 4

And Six Were Kids, and One a Ghostie

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 33–39]

Henry is arrested for Stutgard's murder; the children acquire the Île de France and prepare to take to the waters.

Summary

Shortly after midnight, Sheriff Train arrives with five "hasty deputies" to arrest Henry Dulanty for Stutgard's murder. The sheriff explains: "You aren't liked by the people here. They say you are neither fish nor flesh." Henry asks: "Must I be one or the other?" He could fight: "Did you ever arrest a goblin or ogre who stood six feet four and was as heavy as a yearling ox?" But Earth Allergy has made him listless. "This is their hour," he tells Frank, "and the power of darkness."

Henry tells Frank to put away the bottle and care for the children: the household has lost three adults in three days, to death, derangement, and arrest with intent to lynch. After the arrest, Elizabeth retrieves the bloody axe and hides it. [1968, pp. 33–34]

In the morning, Frank warns the children to stay close to the house. Helen defies him: "A welfare lady will come and take us away. They'll put us in a home, and we'll get stubborn and we won't eat, and we'll all be dead within a week." She notes that their Bagarthach to kill the adults failed. Frank explains: "We shot your Bagarthach down with another one. You can't use them against the Kindred."

The children visit Fulbert Fronsac in the flimsy Lost Haven jail, entering through the roof as they always do. Fulbert greets them: "Misere! There are days when the Good God is not good." He's one of the few who can see Bad John, whom he calls "Ange-Jacques." They acquire a deed to the Île de France; Peter writes it "in a man's hand," joking about the Salic Law, in exchange for a stolen bottle of whisky. Bad John signs with "a different kind of pencil," making a mark invisible to outsiders. The chapter ends with the children sailing away "to be gone forever."

Key Events

  • Henry arrested by Sheriff Train and five deputies; goes peacefully despite Earth Allergy
  • Henry's parting: "three in three days—one dead, one demented, one arrested"
  • Elizabeth hides the bloody axe that night
  • Revelation that Frank and Henry countered Dorothy's Bagarthach: "You can't use them against the Kindred"
  • Children visit Fulbert Fronsac in jail, entering through the roof
  • Bad John identified as witness to Stutgard's murder, but can't testify
  • Helen and John steal whisky as payment for the Île de France
  • Peter writes the deed; Bad John signs with invisible mark
  • Children set sail "to be gone forever"

Characters Introduced

Sheriff Train Fulbert Fronsac Catherine de Medici (goat)

Fulbert Fronsac

❖
The Lost Dauphin

Fulbert is "an old French bum who was also the lost Dauphin. And, if not he, then he was the son of the Dauphin, or the grandson, sometimes the one, sometimes the other." To the town, he's simply the town drunk, the single prisoner in Lost Haven's flimsy tin jail.

Fulbert greets the children with grief and indignation. He intends a serious conversation with God about the misfortune that has struck them. [1968, p. 35]

Fulbert is one of the few who can see Bad John, whom he calls "Ange-Jacques." He owns the Île de France (a fishing raft) and Catherine de Medici (a she-goat "of royal blood", great-great-granddaughter of the first Catherine de Medici, Queen of France).

The Deed to the Île de France

Peter volunteers to write the deed: "I'll write it. It'll look better in a man's hand. Besides, I'm not sure whether the Salic Law obtains in Crow Creek Township."

“To whomever it is respected,” Peter wrote slowly in a solemn voice after taking the paper and pencil. “This is to convey one raft the Île de France with the boathouse and blanket and lantern and automobile horn and the box of snuff and the frying pan and the coffee pot and other accessories in fee simple for one bottle of whisky stolen by Helen and John Dulanty and given in token to Fulbert Fronsac, dated today (I don’t know the date and I bet nobody else does either) and agreeable to all parties.”
— Narrator and Peter’s deed [1968, p. 38]

Helen requires provisions for Catherine’s guest status and freedom to disembark. Charles has the deed witnessed and amended by those present. [1968, p. 38]

Bad John signs with "a different kind of pencil," making a strange mark. Fulbert mutters "something in a tongue older than French," frightened. The mark is invisible to outsiders, though obvious to the children.

Revelations About Bad John

  • Bad John witnessed Crocker kill Stutgard
  • His testimony cannot be used in court; he's invisible and inaudible to most
  • Fulbert can see and hear him
  • "Ange-Jacques could not testify in court. There are advantages as well as disadvantages to invisibility."

On Pucas, Indians, and Fulbert

The Puca (the same as with Indians) were always in rapport with French drunks. And the trouble (again in this case) was just that there weren’t enough French drunks in this part of the country.
— Narrator [1968, p. 35]

Henry's Arrest

Henry allows himself to be arrested despite being able to handle "six shaking men with their rifles." Earth Allergy has made him listless. The men are terrified: "Did you ever arrest a goblin or ogre who stood six feet four and was as heavy as a yearling ox... who could rot the flesh off your bones by making a rime about you?" Yet Henry goes peacefully, "like a confused bull with a new ring in his nose."

When Frank offers to "settle these six quaking lawmen," Henry declines: "But this is their hour, and the power of darkness." Sheriff Train demands: "What kind of talk is that?" Henry answers: "From Luke. He was an Earth writer, but he could almost have made it as a Puca."

Before the arrest, Henry charges Frank with the children’s care and tells him to put the bottle away. He counts the three losses to the household in as many days. [1968, p. 33]

The Children's Plan to Kill Everyone

Their plan is temporarily set aside. As Fulbert asks when they'll need the raft:

"For as long as we like. You see, we're going to kill everybody in the world, and that includes you. You won't be needing the raft any more after that so we're doing you a favor buying it from you."
[1968, p. 38]

Puca Lore

  • Kindred: Frank explains that the adults countered Dorothy’s Bagarthach. [1968, p. 35]
  • Bad John's invisibility: "There are advantages as well as disadvantages to invisibility. And invisibility combined with inaudibility is a combination hard to touch." His testimony cannot help in court.
  • Fulbert’s affinity: he can see and hear Bad John. The narrator connects Pucas and Indians through their rapport with French drunks. [1968, p. 35]
  • Drinking as medicine: Frank's heavy drinking since Veronica's death is described as "a Specific against Earth Allergy."

Notable Quotations

“You aren’t liked by the people here, you know. They say that you are neither fish nor flesh.”
“Must I be one or the other?” Henry asked.
— Sheriff Train and Henry [1968, p. 33]
“But this is their hour,” said Henry, “and the power of darkness.”
“What kind of talk is that?” Sheriff Train demanded.
“From Luke,” said Henry. “He was an Earth writer, but he could almost have made it as a Puca.”
— Henry and Sheriff Train [1968, p. 34]
"A welfare lady will come and take us away. They'll put us in a home, and we'll get stubborn and we won't eat, and we'll all be dead within a week."
— Helen
[1968, p. 34]
“Helen’s the only one that knows what scruples are and she won’t tell us,” John said. “Have we scruples about it, Helen?”
“Not a trace,” Helen affirmed.
— John and Helen [1968, p. 37]
"For as long as we like. You see, we're going to kill everybody in the world, and that includes you."
— Peter to Fulbert
[1968, p. 38]
❧
Scripture at the Arrest

Henry identifies Luke as his source. His “their hour” adapts Christ’s “your hour” in Luke 22:53: he speaks about the arresting men rather than addressing them. [1968, p. 34]

Sources: Luke 22:53.

❧
The Dauphin, the Raft, and the Deed

Fulbert’s lost Dauphin and his Mississippi-bound raft recall the fraudulent king in chapter 19 of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. His goat’s royal name and Peter’s invocation of the Salic Law continue the French dynastic joke. That law concerns royal succession; Peter comically imports it into the question of who should write a local property deed. Fee simple is the deed’s contrasting language of ordinary property ownership. [1968, pp. 35–39]

Sources: Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 19.

❧
An Ode in Reserve

Fulbert’s other alleged father, Le Franc de Pompignan, is the French poet Jean-Jacques Lefranc, marquis de Pompignan (1709–1784), elected to the Académie française in 1759. The claim explains his readiness with writing materials: he might suddenly be taken with an ode. Like his royal descent, it belongs to his shifting pedigree. [1968, p. 37]

Sources: Académie française, Jean-Jacques Lefranc de Pompignan.

← Chapter 3 · Chapter 5 →

The Dulanty Children

Six living children, with Bad John still among them. Their Earth-born immunity is an early assurance, complicated by Peter’s later distress and renewed by Witchy at the end. [1968, pp. 20, 69–71, 142]

◊
On Puca Appearance

"Look at them straight, and you'd hardly notice a thing. But look at them sideways accidentally sometimes, just catching them in the corner of your eye, and they'd scare the liver out of you."

Three children (Elizabeth, Charles, Helen) look "like angels, or like handsome Earthlings." Four (Peter, Dorothy, John, Bad John) look "like potato-faced goblins, like real Pucas." This was planned: "some of the children should look like children of this place, and some of them should look like the children back home."

Elizabeth / Coisreacan-Dia

Age: 9 Appearance: Human Role: Eldest

The eldest and most beautiful. Elizabeth has "the blackest hair and the whitest skin in the world." Unlike her siblings' "potato-faced goblin" appearance, she is "as beautiful as an Earth child," the best-looking of them all, distinguishable as Puca only by "the gleam in her eyes and the way she flicked her ears and crinkled her nose when she talked."

Character Arc

Elizabeth initially favours killing particular enemies rather than everyone. Helen presses her toward the larger scheme. Elizabeth leads the nighttime storytelling and hides the axe after Henry’s arrest; Charles later becomes the family’s acknowledged captain. [1968, pp. 7–9, 25, 34, 138–139]

Key Actions

  • Tells the haunted-picture story of Albert and his unnamed wife (Chapter 1). [1968, pp. 7–9]
  • Slaps fish innards to Stinker heads to fake ear removal (Chapter 5)
  • Commands at Faber raid: "If people knew how much fun this was, everybody would be doing it all the time" (Chapter 6)
  • Discovers Witchy's madness, tells it as "The Floozy" parable (Chapter 3)
  • Hides Crocker’s murder axe after Henry’s arrest; its hiding place is disclosed in Chapter 12. [1968, pp. 34, 108]
  • On Witchy's death: "It's all right, Mama, go ahead and do it" (Chapter 16)

Notable Quotations

“That is all right,” Elizabeth said, “it saves us the trouble.”
— Elizabeth [1968, p. 87]

Puca Name

Coisreacan-Dia: Assumed in Chapter 16. Irish elements suggesting "consecrated to God."

Charles / Laidir

Age: 8 Appearance: Human Role: Patriarch (by end) Title: Earl of the Ears

The steady one who becomes patriarch. Charles belongs with Elizabeth and Helen among the children who look angelic or human; Peter, Dorothy, John, and Bad John have the more obviously goblin-like appearance. After Frank’s death, Charles assumes leadership at eight years old. [1968, pp. 12, 138]

Character Arc

Charles begins as a follower, deferring to Elizabeth and Helen. His mechanical partnership with Peter is established early. He "takes a major step" when he deals with the blackbirders: returning with three pairs of ears and assuming the title "Earl of the Ears." The deaths of the adults change him: he commands the final departure, examines Marshall's corpse "with great curiosity," and leads the family into their new future.

Key Actions

  • Tells the story of the country hotel (Chapter 1)
  • Takes the larger rifle after Peter first holds Jack Fiddler with the .22 (Chapter 5). [1968, pp. 45–46]
  • Disarms blackbirders, returns with ears: "Earl of the Ears" (Chapter 9)
  • Volunteers to build seagoing pandemonium (Chapter 10)
  • Fires at Marshall after Frank's death (Chapter 15)
  • Rolls Marshall’s body into the bog; Marshall has already rolled Frank in (Chapter 15). [1968, pp. 135–138]
  • Commands casting off and the sounding of the horn at the final departure (Chapter 16). [1968, p. 140]

Notable Quotations

“It’s going to be getting a little bit crowded in that bog,” Charles said, “and there aren’t any of them very friendly to each other.”
— Charles, after rolling Marshall into the bog [1968, p. 138]

Puca Name

Laidir: Irish láidir, strong. See Name Translations. [1968, pp. 139–140]

Helen / Lochrann

Age: 6 Appearance: Human Role: Navigator / Strategist

The smallest of the children. Helen is six years old and "the smallest of them all," yet she dominates through force of personality and skill at Bagarthach. She's "the most intelligent of us" (by her own frequent assertion) and is navigator of the Île de France.

Character Arc

Helen is the ideological driver of the extermination plan. She brings Elizabeth and Charles around to killing "everybody in the world." Her Bagarthach verses are the most numerous and effective. She kills Crocker with an early curse. She's also the most theatrical: inventing pirate ships (Spanish Dancer, Vampire, Gigantis Transfixus), distracting the blackbirders with gruesome skull preparation stories, and insisting on social protocol ("In best society, one first speaks of everything else").

Key Actions

  • Tells Silly Jimmy ghost story (Chapter 1)
  • Makes bombs of "chicken dirt and cow dirt and dog dirt and people dirt" (Chapter 5)
  • Tells a pirate adventure naming four ships, including a passing mention of the Flying Snake (Chapter 6). [1968, pp. 52–54]
  • Distracts blackbirders with skull preparation story (Chapter 9)
  • Scalds the lawyer with incandescent tea (Chapter 12)

Bagarthach Verses

Curse on Crocker ☠ Delayed Kill
Old Crocker man, be belled and banged!
You hound-dog hunk, we'll have you hounded!
On else than gallows be you hanged!
In else than water be you drownded!
[1968, p. 15]
Crow-Summoning
I catch you, crow, in curving orb
No matter how you caw and cough you!
I sing the corbie to the corb!
I sing the silly wings right off you!
[1968, p. 23]

Puca Name

Lochrann: Irish lóchrann, lamp or light. The name is linked to Helen’s navigation and intelligence. [1968, pp. 139–140]

Peter / Carraig

Age: 8 Appearance: Goblin Role: Mechanic / Fabricator

The best fabricator. Peter belongs to the goblin-appearing children and is mechanically gifted. He prepares the silencer used by Charles and plans the gears of a seagoing pandemonium. His violent experience of Earth Sickness complicates the children’s supposed immunity. [1968, pp. 12, 69–71, 80–81, 90]

Key Actions

  • Tells the story of Alice and Clarissa, in which Clarissa is carried to Hell (Chapter 1). [1968, pp. 11–12]
  • Sneaks to Lost Haven, builds gadget at shop truck (Chapter 9)
  • Tries to sow discord among blackbirders: "If you knock Harold off in the water..." (Chapter 9)
  • Violent Earth Sickness: slashes himself, plunges underwater (Chapter 8)
  • Will design gears for seagoing pandemonium (Chapter 10)

Bagarthach Verse

Curse on Stutgard ☠ Delayed Kill
Too long, too late you steal and strut;
Your bubble breaks, your grip relaxes!
Beware the under-studding, Stut!
Beware of jackals bearing axes!
[1968, p. 16]

Puca Name

Carraig: Irish carraig, rock. Peter intuits the name during the children’s afternoon revelation. [1968, pp. 139–140]

Dorothy / Feirin-De

Age: 7 Appearance: Goblin Role: Watch / Cook (in training)

The goblin girl who nearly burns down the boat. Dorothy is seven years old and goblin-appearing ("potato-faced goblins, like real Pucas"). She handles key moments, including the Bagarthach that was supposed to kill the adults (but failed because "You can't use them against the Kindred"). She falls asleep on watch when the blackbirders find them.

Key Moments

  • Falls asleep on watch when blackbirders arrive (Chapter 9)
  • Starts fire while heating water; nearly burns down the Île (Chapter 12)
  • Defends John for bringing catfish instead of gun (Chapter 9)
  • States that Charles killed the three missing boys and cut off their ears; Fulbert dismisses the complete accusation (Chapter 12). [1968, pp. 106–107]

Bagarthach Verse

To Kill the Adults (FAILED)
We'll wither Witchy with a prank,
And kindle them in flames like roses—
Veronica and Hank and Frank—
And give them all Apotheosis.
[1968, p. 24]

Puca Name

Feirin-De: plausibly “gift of God”; Irish féirín is a gift or keepsake. [1968, pp. 139–140]

John / Dia-Ta-Caomh

Age: 6 Appearance: Goblin Role: Younger Brother

Six years old, and often paired with his dead brother. John is goblin-appearing and draws the short straw to kill Stutgard. He climbs through the window only to find the man already dead, then takes Crocker’s bloody axe. Helen, also six, is the child the novel explicitly calls the youngest. [1968, pp. 12, 31–32, 55]

Key Moments

  • Draws short straw, must kill Stutgard (Chapter 3)
  • Finds Stutgard already dead, takes wrong axe (Chapter 3)
  • Brings catfish instead of gun: "looks of pure hatred" (Chapter 9)
  • Given the "gory things" (ears) to view by Charles (Chapter 9)

Puca Name

Dia-Ta-Caomh: a constructed name plausibly suggesting that God is kind or gracious. Irish caomh includes dear and gentle. [1968, pp. 139–140]

Bad John / Ionuin

Age: Died as infant Appearance: Translucent Goblin Role: Lookout / Witness

The ghost child. Bad John died as an infant but stays with the family: invisible and inaudible to most people, translucent to those who can perceive him. He "couldn't tell ghost stories, he could only tell people stories, and nobody cares about them." His Puca name is Ionuin, meaning "beloved."

Nature

Bad John can pass into locked rooms and unlatch windows. He is an unreliable lookout because he cannot tell whether it is dark. His absence at the end is explained by Witchy: he has gone with his father Frank. [1968, pp. 30–31, 141]

Key Moments

  • Witnesses Crocker murder Stutgard: Crocker drops axe in terror (Chapter 3)
  • Unlatches door from inside during Faber raid (Chapter 6)
  • Leads Crocker on fatal chase through bogs (Chapter 15)
  • Departs to join Frank: "I believe he's gone for good" (Chapter 16)
"He's no more a ghost than you are. He's scaredest of all of us of ghosts because he can see them oftenest, and they can punch him like they can't do it to us. Bad John is just different because he died when he was a baby."
— Elizabeth
[1968, p. 103]

Puca Name

Ionuin: Irish for "beloved." The name belongs to the ghost child who died as an infant. He is "gone for good" at the novel's end.

Chapter 5

A Child's a Monster Still Uncurled

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 40–46]

The campaign begins: the Stinkers, Stutgard Landing, and Fiddler’s Landing. The other two kingdoms follow in Chapter 6.

Summary

The Dulanty children launch their campaign of conquest in the strip pits: "a dozen square miles of mountains turned inside out, threaded by canals, and with bottomless chasms." The pits remind them of their home world, with its "land and water inextricably mixed" and endless underwater caves. They reason they cannot exterminate the rest of the world while leaving strongholds behind them.

This chapter covers three kingdoms: the Stinkers, Stutgard Landing, and Fiddler’s Landing. Helen’s fire bombs, Peter’s seizure of the .22, and Elizabeth’s use of fish innards make the attacks comic while the intent to kill is real. [1968, pp. 40–46]

The Stinkers survive in shallow water; Amada Stutgard escapes after giving a promise Peter foolishly trusts; Fiddler runs under gunfire. Their survival follows from circumstances and errors. Lanyard Landing and the Fabers belong to the next chapter. [1968, pp. 42–50]

Key Events

  • Battle of Port Stinker: children capture the Sea Bear and a .22 rifle
  • Burning of Stutgard Landing shack; Amada Stutgard escapes
  • Peter pursues Amada but she tricks him and escapes
  • Helen deceived by "Cherokee creeper pods" as ears
  • Raid on Fiddler's Landing: capture whisky, choc beer, ham; Jack Fiddler escapes
  • Next chapter: Lanyard Landing and Phoebe Jane’s hospitality (see Chapter 6). [1968, pp. 47–48]
  • Next chapter: the raid on the Faber stronghold (see Chapter 6). [1968, pp. 49–51]

Characters Introduced

Elwood Elgin (Stinker, 11) Rex Remagen (Stinker) Berny Bottleby (Stinker) Amada Stutgard Jack Fiddler Phoebe Jane Lanyard The Fabers

The Five Kingdoms

✠
1. The Kingdom of the Stinkers

Rulers: Elwood Elgin (11), Rex Remagen, Berny Bottleby

Vessel: The Sea Bear

Taunts exchanged: Elwood: "You look like pigs and you're not people at all." Rex: "You hop like frogs and you eat raw fish." Berny: "You swim like polliwogs and you got tails like them."

Battle: The vessels converge at "more than three miles per hour." Helen hurls Greek fire: paper sacks aflame, filled with "splinters of glass, thumbtacks, cockleburs, cactus, and devil-claws" plus "chicken dirt and cow dirt and dog dirt and people dirt." Peter, "one of the most astute eight-year-old generals in the world," slips overboard, swims under both craft, infiltrates the stockade, and seizes their .22. "Hold, halt, stand, abaft!" he commands. "Ka-zing!" Elizabeth slaps fish innards on each Stinker's head; they believe their ears have been cut off and reattached. She strikes each with a pipe wrench.

Outcome: the attempted drowning fails in shallow water. Helen insists the wounds and contaminated bombs will kill the Stinkers later, but no death is confirmed. The children burn the shack and capture the raft and .22. [1968, pp. 42–43]

✶
2. Stutgard Landing

Status: Nearly abandoned after Coalfactor's death

Action: Shack burned. Amada Stutgard leaps from the rafters where she'd been crying over her father. Helen's command: "Mind you, no mercy. You are instructed to bring back her ears as proof."

Peter’s pursuit: he catches Amada and takes her toward the quicksand. She promises to return after fetching grass, then runs toward her house. From safety she accuses his uncle of killing her father and mocks Peter’s appearance. [1968, pp. 43–44]

Peter's lesson: "Earth people will lie to save their lives and will say a thing when they don't mean it... They are the most treacherous creatures in all the universes."

Outcome: Peter brings Cherokee creeper pods as fake ears. Helen concludes Earth people are "half-plant half-animals" who "generate from seeds"; "Kill them all as fast as we can! They're monsters!"

◆
3. Fiddler's Landing

Ruler: Jack Fiddler (illegal whisky maker, part Quapaw)

Approach: The sheriff never found Fiddler's still, but Catherine de Medici knows the way: "they followed her attitude" as she indicated direction by her posture.

Confrontation: Fiddler covers the children with his larger gun, then leaves it on shore to board the raft and seize them. Peter points the .22 at him; Charles takes the abandoned gun. [1968, pp. 45–46]

Loot: Barrel of corn whisky, barrel of choc beer, tub of mash (Dorothy: "It will be good to eat for breakfast"), a ham. They order him to kneel and pray before dying.

Outcome: Fiddler bolts "whipping and evading like a cotton-tail," dodging bullets from both rifles. Barrels overturned, boat sunk, wagon burned, but house and main stock never found. Helen: "Fashions change in both piracy and liquor" (she'd wanted rum).

❧
4. Lanyard Landing

Chapter 6 preview. Ruler: Phoebe Jane Lanyard (part Shawnee)

Chapter 6 preview. Outcome: No attack. "It is hard to plunder a people who will willingly give you anything they have." Phoebe Jane barters for the whisky, gives them pecans, grape juice, hominy grits, and news of their family. She promises to watch over them.

⁂
5. Faber Stronghold

Chapter 6 preview. Rulers: The Fabers (part Cherokee, commercial fishermen)

Reputation: the Fabers are rumoured to use stray children for bait, but the narrator explicitly says there is no evidence. [1968, p. 49]

Forward reference to Chapter 6: the children burn and wreck the Faber property, then escape in sudden darkness as the Fabers return. [1968, pp. 49–51]

Bagarthach Verses

Helen's Curse on the Stinkers
Oh Stinker limbs that reek and rot,
Stinker head that decomposes!
We'll splatter all the blood you've got,
You seven-letter sos-and-soses!
— Helen, Battle of Port Stinker[1968, p. 41]

Phoebe Jane Lanyard

Forward reference to Chapter 6. Phoebe Jane is introduced as Shawnee, with a comic, expansive genealogy. Her many grandfathers are part of the novel’s tall-tale account. [1968, pp. 47–48]

She's "more Indian than the rest of her family" and has "a way of looking at the Dulantys and chuckling." She can "be as goblin as they could."

Notable Quotations

"The strip pits are a dozen square miles of mountains turned inside out, threaded by canals, and with bottomless chasms."
[1968, p. 40]
“It is no great matter,” Helen said. “What I really want is for you little children to learn tactics, and you learn by your failures.”
— Helen [1968, p. 43]
He learned that Earth people will lie to save their lives and will say a thing when they don’t mean it. Earth people are the most treacherous creatures in all the universes.
— Narrator, through Peter’s offended perspective [1968, p. 44]
“Kids, we don’t know what we got ahold of!” she screeched. “I swear these ears are partly, at least, vegetable fiber.”
— Helen, deceived by Peter’s substitute ears [1968, p. 45]
"We got to start killing people. We can't keep leaving everybody till last."
— Charles, Chapter 6
[1968, p. 49]

Puca Lore

  • Home world: the children compare the pits’ mixture of land and water with the home world they have never seen. [1968, p. 40]
  • Physical clarifications: The children don't hop like frogs but can "jump very high." They do eat raw catfish, though sometimes cook other fish. Swimming is easier "slithering." Their tails are "negligible."
  • Catherine de Medici's knowledge: The goat has watched proper sail rigging countless times but, being a goat, cannot do or explain it. Charles figures it out himself.
❧
Conquest in Miniature

Helen’s burning sacks are called a variant of Greek fire, invoking the incendiary weapon associated with Byzantine warfare. The salting of Stutgard Landing recalls rituals of total destruction. Judges 9:45 records an ancient example in Abimelech’s destruction of Sichem (Shechem). The familiar story of Rome salting Carthage is a disputed later tradition, not a secure ancient precedent; the novel names neither city. [1968, pp. 41–43, 45]

Sources: Judges 9:45; R. T. Ridley, “To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt” (1986).

← Chapter 4 · Chapter 6 →

Chapter 6

The World's a Trap, and None Can Quit It

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 47–56]

A magical night on Green River: ghost ships, pirate adventures, and Helen's tall tales.

Summary

Phoebe Jane’s hospitality frustrates the attack on Lanyard Landing. She warns that Crocker is behind efforts to have the children taken into care, barters for their whisky, and gives them supplies. The children still talk of killing her, but their inability to plunder such generosity makes this encounter different from the others. [1968, pp. 47–48]

They attack "the final principality," the Fabers, commercial fishermen rumored to use stray children as bait. Charles and Peter shoot up the privy ("If there's anybody in there, he's sure dead now"), then storm the shack. Peter cries "Hit the beach! Land ho!" Dorothy asks: "What's so funny about land?" They burn everything, dump hundreds of pounds of fish, slash nets. Elizabeth exults: "If people knew how much fun this was, everybody would be doing it all the time." They escape at sunset, passing the returning Fabers unseen; one oar even strikes the Île but no one notices.

Moored on Green River for "their first night at sea," six strange things happen overnight. Only Helen's story is told: pirate ships ascending the river: the Spanish Dancer, the Vampire, the Gigantis Transfixus. She claims she freed the giant serving as mainmast and sewed her own arms back on. The other children debate whether pirates were invented by Earth people or modeled on Pucas like Blackbeard.

They hide for a day, eating raw fish ("So the taunt of the Stinkers had been right!") and milking Catherine de Medici to mix goat milk with choc beer. Phoebe Jane appears at nightfall, unseen and unheard, scolds them to "stop burning down houses," reports "things look bad" for Frank, Henry, and Witchy, and pilots them to an inlet so dark that "a family lived here for three generations and they never did see the sun." She vanishes into the darkness, leaving only her voice behind.

Key Events

  • Lanyard visit: Phoebe Jane barters whisky for supplies, warns of Crocker's plot
  • Faber raid: privy shot up, shack burned, fish dumped, boathouse torched
  • Escape past returning Fabers, undetected despite oar striking the Île
  • First night moored on Green River: six strange events, only Helen's told
  • Helen's account of the pirate ships (Spanish Dancer, Vampire, Gigantis Transfixus)
  • Debate: pirates as Earth invention vs. Puca model (Blackbeard, Bartholomew Portuguese)
  • Day of hiding: Fabers, Sheriff Train, Crocker with bloodhounds search in vain
  • Raw fish confirms Stinkers' taunt; goat milk mixed with choc beer
  • Phoebe Jane appears unseen, brings supplies, reports on family
  • Phoebe moves them to a darker inlet, described through a tale of a family that lived there without seeing the sun. [1968, pp. 55–56]

The Faber Raid

⚔
The Final Principality

The Fabers know the waters intimately. The children raid their landing while they are absent: Bad John opens the door, and the others burn, slash nets, and dump fish. They escape in sudden darkness as the Fabers return. [1968, pp. 49–51]

Helen's Night: The Pirate Ships

⚓
The Spanish Dancer

"It has the blankest pirates of all on it, except for the Flying Snake." Helen claims they made her captain after recognizing her worth.

✝
The Vampire

"Whose crewmen are served every night a cup of blood with their scuttle of rum." They tested Peter's blood but released him when they discovered he was Puca: "We can't be drinking Puca blood; we got a contract with them."

⛭
The Gigantis Transfixus

In Helen’s account, a giant serves as the mast of the Gigantis Transfixus under a thirty-year spell. His time is already up, though an old calendar has deceived him. Helen says she frees him, survives the destruction, and sews her arms back on; her listeners challenge the details. [1968, pp. 52–54]

The other children are skeptical. Elizabeth interrupts: "Pirates are perhaps the greatest invention of Earth people, and their pirate stories are wonderful entertainment for small children. We have to give Earth people credit for that." Peter counters with Uncle Henry's lore: "Earth people invented pirates, but they used Pucas for a model. Bartholomew Portuguese was a Puca, and so was Teach (Blackbeard)... But the second-rate pirates like Kidd were Earthmen." Helen's accounts grow contradictory. Dorothy asks: "How could you have sewed your right arm on first if you didn't have your left arm on to sew with?" Helen: "I just said that to see if you were paying attention."

Catherine de Medici's Intelligence

Charles fears Catherine’s noise will betray the hiding place, but the goat stays quiet because she would be put in the pot if captured. The children milk her and mix the milk with choc beer. [1968, p. 54]

Phoebe Jane's Supplies

  • Honeycomb and Indian bread
  • A peck of corn and pancake flour
  • A frog fork and gunny sack
  • Pepper and six eggs (she forgot one for Bad John: "I'll bring you two tomorrow night")
  • Shot for the .22 and the .30
  • A blacksnake to play with
  • A bar of soap

Phoebe Jane's News

  • Frank is all right: she told him the children are safe
  • Henry is in jail: she talked to him today
  • Witchy is in the hospital: she saw her "for a little while"
  • "Things look bad for all three of them"

Notable Quotations

"A swift and merciful death is the best we can offer. Don't make us do our worst."
— Peter's terrible cry at Lanyard Landing
[1968, p. 47]
"If people knew how much fun this was, everybody would be doing it all the time."
— Elizabeth, watching the Faber boathouse burn
[1968, p. 50]
"Hit the beach! Land ho!"
"What's so funny about land?"
— Peter and Dorothy
[1968, p. 50]
"So the taunt of the Stinkers had been right! They did eat raw fish! Don't knock it till you've tried it."
[1968, p. 54]
You will have to stay hid. And you have to stop burning down people’s houses. It makes them mad.
— Phoebe Jane [1968, p. 55]
"How could you find us when even the Fabers couldn't?"
"Oh, they're only Cherokees. I wonder God doesn't take their eyes away from them since they never use them."
— Peter and Phoebe Jane
[1968, p. 55]
"It's so dark here that you didn't see me go, and I left my voice here to talk with you for two minutes after I'm gone."
— Phoebe Jane's farewell
[1968, p. 56]
"A-wa-wa-shingay"
— The Dulantys' Shawnee farewell (all the Shawnee words they know)
[1968, p. 56]

Puca Lore

  • Goblin look: Even the human-looking Elizabeth, Charles, and Helen are "taking on the goblin hue" from their time in the pits. Peter: "We can look like regular people till we have to laugh."
  • Puca pirates: Uncle Henry claims Bartholomew Portuguese and Blackbeard were Pucas: "Earth people invented pirates, but they used Pucas for a model." Only second-rate pirates like Kidd were Earthmen.
  • Puca blood contract: The Vampire's crew won't drink Puca blood: "We got a contract with them."
  • Helen as cook: Despite being "the youngest of them all" chronologically, Helen claims seniority in experience. Phoebe: "I forgot just what it is you do mean."
❧
Pirates and Misused Sea Words

Helen names four ships in her account: Spanish Dancer, Flying Snake, Vampire, and Gigantis Transfixus. The Flying Snake receives only a passing mention. Her nautical terms are misused for comic effect: a binnacle normally houses a compass, a davit is a hoisting device, and a scuttle may be a hatch or a container. She rows a binnacle and dips water with a davit. [1968, pp. 51–54]

❧
Historical Names in Family Stories

Bartholomew Portugues, Edward Teach (Blackbeard), and William Kidd were historical pirates or privateers. Peter reports Henry’s classification of the first two as Pucas and Kidd as an Earthman; that classification is family lore. Phoebe Jane’s changing ancestry similarly draws on real figures, including Chouteau, Goodnight, Chisholm, the James brothers, Curtis, Crazy Horse, Payne, and Sequoyah. The incompatible pedigrees are part of her storytelling. [1968, pp. 48, 53–54]

Chapter 7

The "Strife Dulanty" With the World

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 57–65]

Frank Dulanty learns of the coming lynch mob; the nature of the "Strife Dulanty" is revealed.

Summary

Frank Dulanty summons Little Jack Wilson using a Bagarthach "broadcast on the wind." Little Jack warns Frank that the town plans to hang him that very night; he should avoid the shanty at ten o'clock. Little Jack describes the Dulantys' impossible position: "You look almost like everyone else... But, Frank, you are different! And you devil us out of our minds with the difference."

When the mob arrives before ten, Frank slips out through a loosened plank "only he and little Helen knew about" and mingles with them unseen, mimicking their Lost Haven accents. Crocker orders the men to batter the door with a timber, then cunningly twists the knob so they crash inside face-first. Finding nothing, they head for Blind Ben's Bar. Frank re-enters the shanty and finds a noose on his bed with an obscene note from Crocker. His Earth Sickness recedes; Puca power surges. He heads to the bar.

Frank bursts in. Sad Sam Burns gasps: "Holy horse-hocks! It's The Dulanty!" Frank throws the noose over a rafter and captures Crocker, forcing him to eat the insulting note until he nearly strangles. He empties Crocker's billfold to pay for everyone's drinks ("Everybody drinks but Crocker") and then orders Crocker to leave with the noose still around his neck and the rope trailing behind him. Frank stays to entertain the men, but feels Earth Allergy creeping back.

Meanwhile, Phoebe Jane visits Witchy at the institution in Vinita. Witchy's eyes don't focus; the two sides of her face are different. She recites mocking verses about the Devil, Crocker, and Stutgard, breaks cups and spoons, and asks for Veronica to bring coffee, forgetting Veronica is dead. She begs Phoebe to contact "others of our sort": Willy McGilly, Diogenes Pontifex, John Pandemonium, Aloysius Shiplap. Then she seizes, foams, raves. Attendants restrain her. She never asks about the children.

Key Events

  • Frank summons Little Jack Wilson via Bagarthach, learns of lynching plan
  • Mob arrives before ten; Frank escapes through loose plank Helen knew about
  • Frank mingles with mob unseen, mimicking Lost Haven accents
  • Crocker's men batter the door; he tricks them into crashing inside
  • Frank finds noose and obscene note on his bed; Puca power surges
  • Showdown at Blind Ben's Bar: Frank captures Crocker with the noose
  • Crocker forced to eat the note; billfold emptied for drinks
  • Crocker sent away with noose trailing, publicly humiliated
  • Phoebe Jane visits Witchy at Vinita institution
  • Witchy recites Devil/Crocker/Stutgard verses, asks about "others of our sort"
  • Witchy seizes and is restrained; never asks about the children

Characters Introduced

Little Jack Wilson Joe Cottonhead Blind Ben Sad Sam Burns

The Showdown at Blind Ben's Bar

⚖
Frank's Triumph

Joe Cottonhead, afraid of the Dulantys but also afraid of the mob, helps Frank by announcing free drinks at Blind Ben's. Frank arrives with explosive force, holding the noose intended for his own neck. He throws it over a rafter and captures Crocker.

Crocker babbles: "Some of you men take this fool! Sad Sam, you've got your rifle—" Frank silences him by tightening the rope. He shows the obscene note: "If you wrote it, eat it." Crocker denies it, but the men confirm. Frank forces him to swallow it, nearly strangling him.

Blind Ben supplies the drinks. Frank takes Crocker’s money to pay for the gathering while denying Crocker a drink. He then sends Crocker home with the noose on and the rope trailing. [1968, pp. 61–63]

The "Strife Dulanty"

Little Jack’s warning names the townspeople’s fear of the Dulantys’ difference. That fear operates alongside concrete hostility, the planned lynching, and the corrupt interests later disclosed by Marshall. [1968, pp. 57–58, 94–95]

"You look almost like everyone else, and damned if you don't act almost like everyone else—and I like you and your kindred better than I like anyone else in town. You've treated me decently and made me feel like a person, but I'm the butt of the lowest Lost Haven clown of them all. But, Frank, you are different! And you devil us out of our minds with the difference."
[1968, p. 57]

Frank's Condition

The townspeople believe Frank is still drunk, but he's been sober for two days. His staggering is from Earth Allergy:

He wavered in his walk like a drunk, and he had the flushed look and the hot eye of a drunk. But he was sober as a Rogers County judge. It was the Earth Allergy that had caught up with him and sent him along reeling and sick, that would kill him soon if something else didn’t do it first.
— Narrator on Frank [1968, p. 58]

Bagarthach Summoning

First demonstration of using Bagarthach to summon a specific person:

"Little Jack Wilson... came and talked to Frank Dulanty one afternoon in the hills away from town. Little Jack didn't know how he had happened to meet Frank there, or even how he happened to be walking in the hills. But Frank knew. He had summoned Little Jack by means of a Bagarthach verse broadcast on the wind. You slant your verse to the man you are calling, and it will bring him almost every time."
[1968, p. 57]

On Puca and Death

"I'm told that you, whatever you are, do not fear death."
"Oh, we don't mind going when it's time to go, Little Jack. But we don't like being told by our lessers that it's time to go. And this hanging, for personal reasons I wish to avoid it. I tell you, any man or group that wants to hunt us like prey, we make it an interesting hunt."
[1968, p. 58]

Phoebe Jane Visits Witchy

At the institution in Vinita, Witchy's "eyes did not focus properly. The two sides of her face were different." She recites verses she claims are from Scripture but clearly invented. She breaks cups and bends spoons, demands coffee from Veronica (forgetting Veronica is dead), and begs Phoebe to help her escape "over the wall after dark."

Witchy asks Phoebe to find other Pucas, naming Willy McGilly, Diogenes Pontifex, John Pandemonium, and Aloysius Shiplap. Their contacts are informal and intuitive. She then suffers a fit and is restrained, without asking about the children. [1968, pp. 64–65]

Witchy's Devil Verses

Witchy's First Verse
The Devil and Crocker and Stut
Put all of their heads in one hat,
And mixed them and added them up,
And hadn't the brains of a cat.
— Witchy, claiming it's from Saint John[1968, p. 64]
Witchy's Second Verse
The Devil sent Crocker for Stut
To bring him his head on a plate.
The Devil said 'I'm in a rut,
That's something I oughtn't to ate.'
— Witchy, "in the manner of Tertullian"[1968, p. 64]
Witchy's Final Verse
The Devil rolled Stut like a ball
And said as he dropped in a hole,
'It tickles my tail to recall
The prices he charged us for coal.'
— Witchy's last words before being led away[1968, p. 65]

Notable Quotations

You have no friends here. I’d like to be, but I’m scared on both sides: scared of you because I don’t understand what kind of thing you are, and scared of the men of Lost Haven who will chop down anything that attaches to you.
— Little Jack Wilson [1968, p. 57]
"You look almost like everyone else, and damned if you don't act almost like everyone else... But, Frank, you are different! And you devil us out of our minds with the difference."
— Little Jack Wilson
[1968, p. 57]
“Holy horse-hocks!” breathed Sad Sam Burns. “It’s The Dulanty!”
— Sad Sam Burns [1968, p. 61]
“Keep the drinks coming till it’s used up,” he told Blind Ben. “Crocker promised these men a show tonight, and this is the least he can do for them.”
— Frank [1968, p. 62]
"Go home now, Crocker. But leave the noose around your neck and the rope trailing you in the street."
— Frank Dulanty
[1968, p. 63]

Puca Lore

  • Bagarthach summoning: "You slant your verse to the man you are calling, and it will bring him almost every time." First demonstration of using Bagarthach to summon a specific person.
  • Puca mimicry: Frank mingles with the mob by perfectly imitating their Lost Haven accents; Puca can pass among humans when needed.
  • Power surge: When Frank finds the noose and note, "Earth Sickness recedes; Puca power rises." The "mean crooked grin" surfaces, a dangerous aura that makes Crocker's dogs cower.
  • Other Pucas: Witchy names several wandering contacts and asks Phoebe to find them through intuitive means. [1968, p. 65]
❧
Judgment and Counterfeit Authorities

Little Jack’s sheep and goats recall Matthew 25:32, while his warning that Frank’s life will be required recalls Luke 12:20. Witchy, meanwhile, attributes her invented verses to Saint John and Tertullian, and Phoebe challenges her. The head demanded on a plate echoes the Baptist’s death in Matthew 14:8. [1968, pp. 58–59, 64–65]

❧
Other Lafferty Characters

Witchy’s list connects this novel with Lafferty’s recurring scientific company: Willy McGilly, Diogenes Pontifex, and Aloysius Shiplap also appear around the Institute for Impure Science in “Thus We Frustrate Charlemagne.” In that story Pontifex is excluded from membership under the Minimal Decency Rule. A shared name is a cross-reference. [1968, p. 65]
