Chapter 8

Was Mostly That They Didn't Fit It

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 66–74]

The children explore Misu Mound and its ghostly inhabitants; Peter suffers Earth Sickness; a priest hears Henry's confession and dies.

Summary

Smoke from the dead’s chamber haunts the river bend. Helen and Peter dispute the meaning of left and right banks. Helen’s explanation is deliberately muddled; Peter answers with a joke about her brain. [1968, pp. 66–69]

Phoebe’s mound lore includes successive peoples and companion animals. Her uncle brings anomalous bones to university professors, whose explanation dismisses them as a composite hoax. The narrator mocks their confidence and unwillingness to excavate. [1968, pp. 66–68]

The children discover a secret room fifty feet below where the old dead gather to talk, crack bones for marrow, and smoke heavily (causing the fog). They befriend these Indian ghosts, learn Earth customs, and place two skulls on their raft prows. Meanwhile, Peter suffers violent Earth Sickness before dawn, a "passion" that drives him to slash himself on brush, plunge underwater until his lungs nearly burst, and swim for an hour. He notices Helen may share the same affliction; both are frightened by this.

An old Dutch priest finds Henry reading Job. Henry treats Earth scripture as comparative mythology and speaks of the Anointed, whom the Puca generally do not believe has yet been born. The priest wonders whether salvation extends to intelligent aliens. Henry’s confession overwhelms him: the narrator says it kills him, and reports his death in the Old Priests’ Home a month later. [1968, pp. 71–74]

Key Events

  • Helen and Peter's left/right bank argument ("international covenant")
  • Misu Mound lore: pre-Shawnee burials with companion animals
  • Phoebe Jane's uncle's bones rejected by professors as a hoax
  • Children discover secret room 50 feet below; befriend old Indian ghosts
  • Dead smoke pipes constantly (causing the fog), crack bones, drink corn beer
  • Two skulls placed on raft prows
  • Peter's pre-dawn Earth Sickness: violent passion, self-harm, underwater submersion
  • Helen may share the affliction; both are frightened
  • Dutch priest visits Henry in jail; theological exchange about Puca origins
  • Henry confesses; priest's mind destroyed; dies one month later

Characters Introduced

The Dutch Priest Professor Elmo Phoebe Jane's Uncle

Misu Mound

⛰
The Layered Burials

Phoebe’s account ranges through burials with horses, lions, bears, and buffalo, with unknown things below. She also claims a Puca layer; the narrator rejects that claim as an addition meant to provoke the children. [1968, pp. 66–68]

In the mound story, further burials cease when the crowded dead protest. The voices and noises of its occupants leave unclear who, or what, is buried there. [1968, p. 68]

💀
The Secret Room

Fifty feet below the mound's peak, accessible only through passages the children have learned, lies a chamber where the dead gather. They talk, crack bones for marrow, drink corn beer, and smoke constantly; the smoke vents through a hole, causing the perpetual fog. The children befriend these "old Indians," learning forgotten Earth customs and the art of pipe-smoking.

Peter's Earth Sickness

Two hours before dawn, a violent "passion" rises from the ground or water: "too early, too green, too rank." Peter flees his sea-hammock trembling, crashes through thickets, slashes himself on brush, tastes his own blood. He plunges underwater, grabbing mud at the bottom, staying until "even Puca lungs were near to bursting." He swims for over an hour, trying to exhaust the sensation.

Afterward, he avoids physical closeness with Elizabeth and Helen. He observes his cousins: none show the passion except possibly Helen. When their eyes meet, both are frightened by what they recognize in each other.

Henry's Confession

✝
The Priest's Visit

An old "Holland Dutchman" priest finds Henry reading Job in St. Jerome's Vulgate: "Maerens incedebam sine furore, consurgens in turba clamabam." The priest calls Job "the Majestic Cry-Baby." Henry: "We luxuriate in our misfortunes more than Earth folk."

Henry and the priest discuss Puca visits to Earth, biblical giants, angels, and the Anointed. Henry says most Pucas think the Anointed has not yet been born. The priest’s question about alien salvation is left unresolved. [1968, pp. 71–73]

Henry explains an ordered hierarchy of confessors: Sagart, Puca, inhabitant of Astrobe, inhabitant of Camiroi, Earthman, dromedary, dog, mole, tree, stone. His warning about the burden of Puca confession is fulfilled by the priest’s collapse and death a month later. [1968, pp. 73–74]

Notable Quotations

When you face downriver, the left bank is the left bank. But when you turn around and face upriver, then the left bank is the right bank and the right bank is the left bank.
— Helen’s muddled bank explanation [1968, p. 66]
"The only place it is still the left bank when it is on your right is in the left lobe of your brain. I suspect the Helen-brain is mostly left lobe."
— Peter
[1968, p. 66]
“Oh, go away and leave us alone,” the old dead people grumbled, “we’re full up here.”
— The old dead in the mound’s story [1968, p. 68]
Yes, we confess. Try and stop one of us sometime. As we come to our end, we are not the Majestic Cry-Babies, but we are the most Bumptious Babblers you ever encountered.
— Henry to the priest [1968, p. 73]

Puca Lore

  • Mound affinity: the children recall their mothers’ stories of mounds back home. The resemblance connects them with Misu Mound. [1968, pp. 68–69]
  • Earth Sickness in youth: Peter’s violent passion troubles the early account of immunity. The narrative relates it to growth and Earth’s effect on the children; Witchy later offers a renewed assurance. [1968, pp. 69–71, 142]
  • Puca confession: Pucas approaching death become "Bumptious Babblers" who confess to anyone: priest, dog, or stone. Their confessions hold "deeper and darker places" than human sins.
  • Fear-ungadh-mac: the Anointed in Henry’s account of Puca teaching. His discussion with the priest tests the relation between that expectation and Christian salvation. [1968, pp. 71–73]
  • Biblical giants: The priest asks if Pucas are the giants of Genesis. Henry agrees some Pucas have visited Earth across millennia.
❧
The Language of Earth Sickness

Peter’s suffering is described through substance and accidentals, terms associated with scholastic distinctions between a being and what inheres in it. Anima means soul; matrix means womb. The Puca soul in an Earth matrix is a picture of development in an unsuitable environment. The vocabulary returns when Pandemonium describes Witchy’s confusion of essence and accidence. [1968, pp. 70, 86–87]

Sources: “Accident,” Catholic Encyclopedia.

❧
The Priest’s Scriptural Conversation

Henry reads Job 30:28 in Latin. The priest’s continuation draws selectively on verses 29–31. Other references are Genesis 6:4 (giants), 1 Corinthians 6:3 (judging angels), and John 1:46: Henry substitutes Earth for Nazareth. The small birthplace of the Anointed recalls Micheas (Micah) 5:2. His geographical label Coelo-Syria is loose: Bethlehem is in Judaea, not in the narrow valley usually called Coele-Syria. [1968, pp. 71–73]

Sources: Job 30:28–31, Douay-Rheims.

❧
Confession Beyond the Priest

Henry’s descending list of confessors begins with a recognizable theological case. The Summa permits confession to a layperson in necessity, but distinguishes that act from priestly absolution and requires confession to a priest when one becomes available. Henry extends the list through other peoples and then animals, a tree, and a stone. The extension goes beyond the theological rule. Astrobe recalls Past Master; the Camiroi recur in “Primary Education of the Camiroi” and “Polity and Custom of the Camiroi.” [1968, pp. 73–74]

Sources: Aquinas, Summa theologiae, Supplement, q. 8, a. 2.

← Chapter 7 · Chapter 9 →

The Dulanty Adults

Two brothers married two sisters: Henry and Witchy are parents of Elizabeth, Charles, and Helen; Frank and Veronica are parents of Peter, Dorothy, John, and Bad John. All four adults die by the end, though Henry and Frank are killed while suffering Earth Sickness. [1968, pp. 12, 17, 33, 126–144]

†
Earth Allergy

"The Earth Sickness has caught me." Earth Allergy is fatal to adult Puca. It attacks the liver and kidneys ("the seat of good humor") and taints one with the "Earth outlook." Symptoms include flushing, wavering gait (resembling drunkenness), and progressive weakness. Children born on Earth are largely immune.

Henry Dulanty

Role: Father/Uncle Status: Murdered Death: Chapter 14

The stronger brother, wrongly accused. Henry is the more vigorous of the two Dulanty men, though Earth Allergy has sapped his strength. He is arrested for Stutgard's murder (a crime actually committed by Crocker) and eventually murdered by Marshall and Crocker at the Butterfield farm.

Character Arc

Henry allows himself to be arrested despite being able to handle "six shaking men with their rifles." His listlessness comes from Earth Allergy. In jail, he has a pivotal confrontation with Marshall where he reveals Puca history and threatens the "dragons' eggs" they've planted. He escapes jail but is recaptured and killed.

Key Moments

  • Tells Frank to "put the bottle away" before arrest (Chapter 4)
  • Confronts Marshall in jail: physical fight (Chapter 11)
  • Escapes at 8:55 p.m. using Frank’s key and a Bagarthach (Chapter 12). [1968, pp. 109–111]
  • Aided by Indians at Lost Moon Bar (Chapter 13)
  • Shot three times by Marshall; Crocker fires the fatal shot into his face at Butterfield’s farm (Chapter 14). [1968, pp. 126–127]

Bagarthach Verse

Curse on Marshall ☠ Prophetic Kill
Oh Mandrake man, of giants bred,
You didn't guess one singing trifle
Would ever enter in your head—
A message from a talking rifle.
— Fulfilled when Phoebe Jane shoots Marshall[1968, p. 95]

On Dragons' Eggs

"We've laid dragons' eggs behind us. They're hatched and going now. You'll not know the young while they're growing. They are a time bomb in you."
[1968, p. 92]

Death

Shot repeatedly by Marshall in a prolonged, sadistic killing. Final shot to the face by Crocker. "The Dulantys could manage to look like regular people, till they had to laugh, or die."

Frank Dulanty

Role: Father/Uncle Status: Murdered Death: Chapter 15

The grieving brother who finds his strength. Frank drinks after Veronica’s death, but his later drunken appearance is expressly attributed to Earth Allergy when he is sober. He humiliates Crocker with the noose, makes Henry’s escape key, and dies during the final confrontation. [1968, pp. 22, 58, 63, 109, 135]

Character Arc

Frank’s grief, drinking, illness, and force of will coexist. He summons Little Jack Wilson, confronts Crocker, and makes the key for Henry’s escape. Before his last confrontation, he intends to urge the children toward gentleness and a broader way of dealing with the world. He is killed before he can give that counsel. [1968, pp. 57–65, 109, 134–135]

Key Moments

  • Counters Dorothy’s Bagarthach with Henry, as Frank explains in Chapter 4. [1968, p. 35]
  • Summons Little Jack Wilson via Bagarthach (Chapter 7)
  • Places the noose around Crocker’s neck at Blind Ben’s Bar (Chapter 7). [1968, pp. 61–63]
  • Makes the key used in Henry’s escape (Chapter 12). [1968, p. 109]
  • Hunts Crocker through the bogs (Chapter 15)

On His Condition

"He wavered in his walk like a drunk, and he had the flushed look and the hot eye of a drunk. But he was sober as a Rogers County judge. It was the Earth Allergy that had caught up with him."
[1968, p. 58]

Death

Killed by Marshall from behind with "a terrific blow on the back of the head with his rifle butt" while attempting to hang Crocker. "The blow was one of the really colossal things."

Veronica

Role: Mother Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 2 (backstory)

The center of the two families. Veronica is Frank’s wife, mother of Peter, Dorothy, John, and Bad John, and Witchy’s sister. Her death from Earth Allergy precipitates the household’s collapse. [1968, pp. 17–22, 33]

Character

Veronica is described as practical and central to family cohesion. She tells the characteristic Aorach story of how she and Witchy were "twins" born eleven months apart. Her death is the first major tragedy, leading to Frank's drinking and Witchy's madness.

The Aorach of Her Conception

An Earth doctor, who treated Veronica (unsuccessfully) for Earth Allergy, told Veronica that such a thing was impossible, that twins could not be born eleven months apart. Imagine an Earth doctor trying to tell a mistress of the Aorach about something as fundamental as that.
— Narrator [1968, p. 19]

Last Words

“I can’t very die just yet,” was the last thing she said. “Witchy is going out of her wits and she needs me. If I die, the family will break up.”
— Veronica; “very die” is the copy-text reading [1968, p. 22]

Death

Veronica dies two days before Henry’s arrest. The six-week interval refers to the families’ residence in Lost Haven, not the time since her death. [1968, pp. 15, 33]

Witchy / Briochtog

Role: Mother Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 16

The unearthly beauty who goes mad. Witchy is the more ethereal of the two sisters, possessed of an "unearthly beauty" that marks her as distinctly Puca. After Veronica's death, she descends into madness and is hospitalized. She escapes to deliver her final charge to the children before dying aboard the Île de France.

Character Arc

Witchy's madness is discovered by Elizabeth in Chapter 3 (told parabolically as "The Floozy"). She is hospitalized, described as being in an asylum. In the final chapter, she boards the departing raft to deliver her charge to the children, then dies of Earth Allergy.

The Final Charge

There isn’t any way to live in accord with this World as it is, children. You will have to chance it here and there, and sometimes you will have to excise elements that seem important to Earth people. It’s a stubborn and worthless old animal the way it is. Break it.
— Witchy; “chance” is the copy-text reading [1968, p. 143]
"I break the egg! I turn you loose! Oh, my own Dragons' Seed!"
[1968, p. 144]

On the Primitive Ethic

"Ourselves, we live by a more primitive ethic. We do not deny that it is primitive, but it is the only ethic that the Giver has given us yet. We live that primitive ethic all the way. Be swift, and be sudden! That is our secret."
[1968, p. 141]

Puca Name

Briochtog: Dinneen’s briochtóg, witch or sorceress. [1968, p. 143]

Death

Dies aboard the Île de France after delivering her charge. "It's all right, Mama, go ahead and do it. Don't give it another thought." Her eyes fade to "a fainter green" alongside her children's glowing eyes in the final image.

Continue to: Antagonists →

Chapter 9

No Setting For the Gallant Brood

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 75–81]

The children accept their parents as "ancestors"; Crocker's blackbirders find them, but Charles handles it.

Summary

The children treat the parents as already passing into ancestry: Veronica is dead, Witchy confined, Henry threatened, and Frank ill. Their comparison with a Puca comedy of successive quicksand deaths anticipates the later bog sequence. [1968, p. 75]

Peter sneaks back to Lost Haven, disguised as a "blank-faced Earth kid," and builds a gadget at the Dulanty shop truck. He gives it to Charles. Meanwhile, Crocker, frustrated that Sheriff Train and his bloodhounds failed, hires local children as "blackbirders" at a dollar a day: Baxter Bushyhead and Little Sad Sam Jones ("really big boys with shotguns") plus middle-sized Harold Harvestman with a carbine.

The blackbirders catch the Dulantys sleeping; even their watch Dorothy has dozed off. "We got you cold!" But Helen distracts Baxter with gruesome talk of skull preparation: severing heads, removing ears for turtle bait, brains for catfish. When she tells John to "show them the big catfish we caught with those last brains," he brings out catfish instead of a gun, earning looks of "pure hatred" from his siblings. Peter elaborates: "Eyes are the best bait of all. We catch garfish with them." Charles, instructed to fetch "a three-foot-long garfish," returns with the .30 rifle and disarms the blackbirders.

Charles takes the captives into the woods and returns with money and three pairs of ears. He says he killed them with a silenced gun; the narrator confirms that Peter made a silencer. In Chapter 12, Dorothy explicitly says Charles killed them. Together these point to offstage killings that the narrator never shows. [1968, pp. 79–81, 106]

Key Events

  • Children accept parents as effectively dead: "metamorphosis" into ancestors
  • Peter sneaks to Lost Haven, builds gadget at shop truck
  • Crocker hires blackbirders: Baxter Bushyhead, Little Sad Sam Jones, Harold Harvestman
  • Blackbirders catch sleeping Dulantys; even Dorothy the watch dozed
  • Helen's skull preparation distraction: ears, brains, eyes as bait
  • John's error: brings catfish instead of gun: "looks of pure hatred"
  • Charles disarms blackbirders with .30 rifle
  • Charles marches captives into woods, returns with money and "three pairs" of ears
  • Peter dubs Charles "Earl of the Ears"

Characters Introduced

Baxter Bushyhead Little Sad Sam Jones Harold Harvestman

The Blackbirders

⚔
Crocker's Hired Hunters

Baxter Bushyhead and Little Sad Sam Jones are "really big boys", eleven years old but "big as a house." Harold Harvestman is middle-sized and spindly, Baxter's cousin. Crocker pays them a dollar a day to find the Dulanty children after Sheriff Train and the bloodhounds failed.

Little Sad Sam calculates excitedly: "We get a nine dollar bonus! That's a woolly bunch of money." Peter tries to sow discord: "If you knock Harold off in the water and hold him under while he drowns, you'll each get four dollars and a half." Baxter refuses: "Ah, we hadn't better, he's my cousin."

Helen's Skull Distraction

Helen criticizes Baxter's skull shape: "What a pity you're imperfect." She claims they collect skulls from enemies and explains the gruesome preparation:

  • Sever heads, remove ears (turtle bait)
  • Remove brains (catfish bait)
  • Remove eyes (garfish bait: "the best bait of all")
  • Boil skulls, mount on raft prows

Peter elaborates: "You won't have anything left to see it with. We'll have your eyes in the eye jug, and you won't be in your skull anymore."

Notable Quotations

After your parents die they turn into your ancestors.
— Helen [1968, p. 75]
Come on shore and start marching.
— Baxter Bushyhead [1968, p. 77]
I used a silencer.
— Charles; the narrator later confirms the device [1968, pp. 79–81]
"I don't know why you got mad at John. You told him to get the catfish. If you wanted him to get a gun, why didn't you tell him so?"
— Dorothy, defending John
[1968, p. 81]

Puca Lore

  • Puca comedy: The children compare their parents' fate to "old Puca comedies": one falls into quicksand and pulls others in after. Earth is replaying this scenario.
  • Peter the fabricator: "Peter was a better fabricator than any of the rest of them"; he builds gadgets and devices while others search for them.
  • Charles's transformation: "Charles had taken a major step. You can't remain a child forever." The severed ears mark his crossing a line.
❧
Children as Press Gangs

Blackbirders and impressors carry histories of coerced labor and forced recruitment. Applied to children hired to capture other children, they mark Crocker’s bounty system as coerced recruitment. Harold Harvestman’s name also makes a visual joke: a harvestman is a daddy longlegs. Baxter Bushyhead’s surname has Cherokee historical associations, but the boy has no identified historical namesake. [1968, pp. 76–81]

Chapter 10

In Sacred Groves of Yew or Lindens

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 82–90]

Pandemonium John arrives with his rolling castle of instruments; the children learn their parents' fates and hold a grand "honkeroo."

Summary

The children wake to an inward horn, the sort Veronica associated with Bagarthachs from home. Birds and fish react to the approaching sound. Charles imagines burning horses and a ready meal; Helen recognizes music. Pandemonium John arrives amid the noise, singing the nine violent stanzas transcribed in the verse collection. [1968, pp. 82–85]

The children cry in unison: "Pandemonium John!" He is a high Eigeas-Amhranai, a legendary Puca singer surpassing "Homer, Dante, and Shakespeare combined." Too old and Earth-sick to disguise himself, he travels a nine-state area forcing towns to pay him to leave. His pandemonium is "a crazy cat-castle of shining silver and gold, or of brass and chrome," with a resonator that transmits messages to the home world.

John has exchanged Bagarthachs with the parents, including the recently dead Veronica. He brings their news himself: Frank’s race against sickness and enemies, Henry’s hopeless defiance, and Witchy’s likely death within about a week. Elizabeth accepts the news with relief. The news comes by Bagarthach; the resonator is a separate part of John’s apparatus. [1968, pp. 86–89]

They launch a grand "honkeroo": a wild jam session through afternoon and night. Pucas can play any instrument instinctively. They mix Earth songs ("Birmingham Jail Blues," "Shotgun Boogie," "Rang-Dang-Doo") with Puca music. Pandemonium John drinks half a barrel of choc beer. Charles volunteers to build a "seagoing pandemonium"; Peter will design gears that play "The Old Apple Tree in the Orchard" at normal speed and "Bell-Bottomed Trousers" when accelerated. Elizabeth and Helen trade murderous Bagarthach verses about each other.

Key Events

  • Internal "horn off Earth" wakes children: crows and catfish react
  • Pandemonium John arrives with his rolling castle of instruments
  • Revealed as high Eigeas-Amhranai, legendary Puca singer
  • Brings Bagarthach news: Frank dying, Henry doomed, Witchy insane, Veronica's final message
  • Elizabeth: "That saves us the trouble"
  • Grand "honkeroo": jam session through afternoon and night
  • Charles volunteers to build seagoing pandemonium
  • Elizabeth and Helen trade murderous verses about each other

Pandemonium John

♫
The High Eigeas-Amhranai

John’s apparatus is enormous and was once dismantled by investigators looking for a transmitter. The narrator reveals that it does communicate by cosmic resonance. Forty or fifty instruments describes the smaller version proposed for Charles. [1968, pp. 88–89]

His verses reference a deceased Earth wife and daughter who couldn't adapt to Puca ways. He survives by playing until towns pay him to leave: "There are towns in my nine-state area that haven't heard the shrill of my pandemonium for twenty years."

Pandemonium John's Philosophy

As Pucas, you do not have to be either good or careful.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 87]

Bagarthach Verses

Elizabeth's Verse About Helen
I had a little sister dear
As pretty as a springtime crocus.
I buried her without a tear,
She was a little too pre-co-cus.
[1968, p. 90]
Helen's Verse About Elizabeth
I also had a sister sweet,
I worshiped her, I idolized her,
Until I put her on to heat,
And accidentally vaporized her.
[1968, p. 90]

Notable Quotations

Frank tells me in verse that it is a race: which will kill him first, the Sickness, or the alien creatures who look like people.
— Pandemonium John reporting Frank [1968, p. 86]
Witchy is sometimes in a state where she confuses essence with accidence. The Earth people have a humorous name for the state—insanity.
— Pandemonium John [1968, pp. 86–87]
“That is all right,” Elizabeth said, “it saves us the trouble.”
— Elizabeth [1968, p. 87]

Puca Lore

  • Eigeas-Amhranai: John’s title as master of song. The narrator’s comparison draws on poets, musicians, and singers from many traditions and rejects a Cameroi critic’s dismissal. [1968, pp. 85–86]
  • Instinctive music: "Pucas can play instinctively any instrument whether they have ever seen it before or not."
  • Resonator: The pandemonium transmits to the home world, not electronically, but through some Puca mechanism.
  • Bagarthach from the dead: Veronica, "dead and buried, but not so long dead she cannot receive and send back Bagarthachs."
❧
Milton’s Name, John’s Noise

Pandæmonium is the capital of Satan and his peers in Paradise Lost. The later sense of uproar suits both John and his rolling apparatus. His title Eigeas-Amhranai joins Irish words for a learned person or poet and a singer. The catalogue of Homer, Dante, the Edda, Shakespeare, the Psalms, Pindar, and popular musicians sets his art beside the whole range of song. It also uses the racist historical label “coon-shouter” and a derogatory description of German composers. “Benny B-Flat” is unidentified. [1968, pp. 84–86]

Sources: Milton, Paradise Lost 1.756–57.

❧
Goodness and Caution

John reverses “If you can’t be good, be careful” before rejecting both requirements for Pucas. A related Latin maxim, si non caste, tamen caute, advises caution when chastity is absent. Aquinas cites that maxim in his commentary on Ephesians 5:15 in order to reject it as Paul’s meaning. [1968, p. 87]

Sources: Aquinas, Super Ephesios, ch. 5, lect. 6.

❧
The Songs of Earth

The honkeroo’s repertoire joins “Birmingham Jail Blues,” “Take Me Back to Tulsa,” “Shotgun Boogie,” “Red River Valley,” and “Rang-Dang-Doo.” The phrase about being too young to marry continues the Tulsa song. “Shotgun Boogie” is Tennessee Ernie Ford’s song, recorded on July 27, 1950. “The Old Apple Tree in the Orchard” has no secure identification; the familiar “In the Shade of the Old Apple Tree” is a possible comparison. [1968, pp. 88–89]

Sources: Tennessee Ernie Ford, official singles discography.

← Chapter 9 · Chapter 11 →

✦The Arrival Songs

The nine opening stanzas and John’s advertisement are transcribed with the other verses in Bagarthach Verses. His opposed proverbs are “If you can’t be good, be careful” and “If you can’t be careful, be good.” The replacement heads are the children, “in a manner of speaking.”

[1968, pp. 82–88]

Chapter 11

They Found a Hold More Near Their Blood

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 91–97]

Mandrake Marshall reveals his nature and his plans; the War of the Worlds begins.

Summary

Mandrake Marshall visits Henry Dulanty in the poorly-run jail. "I like to come to the point. You're a dead man, Dulanty. Man, Hell! I consider you an animal, and I'll kill you for one." Marshall demands to know Henry's species. Henry answers: "Homo Pucalis—Puca Man." Marshall recalls a museum prank two years ago when an unidentified specimen labeled "Puca Man" appeared in the Anthropological Museum. Henry confirms he placed his kinsman's body there: "We have more fun at our burials and disposals than you do."

Marshall reveals his backstory: illiterate miner at seventeen, sent to college by Stutgard to play football for eight years. He learned to read in a month, gained total recall, bullied the state legislature as house whip, then became prosecutor. He explains Lost Haven's corruption: Stutgard shrank the population to exploit relief checks and fake crop claims: "bogus relief checks might run around sixty thousand dollars a month."

Henry warns that the Pucas have left dragons’ eggs on Earth. He argues that a people so few in number must become a dominant elite or perish. Marshall refuses that prospect. Henry’s Bagarthach anticipates a rifle message entering Marshall’s head. [1968, pp. 92–95]

Marshall attacks Henry with a sap. Henry drives him from the cell after a fight the narrator calls a war of the Worlds. Marshall is badly beaten but leaves laughing, confident that he has other ways to defeat Henry. [1968, pp. 96–97]

Key Events

  • Marshall visits Henry: "I consider you an animal, and I'll kill you for one"
  • Henry identifies as "Homo Pucalis—Puca Man"
  • Museum prank revealed: Henry placed kinsman's body in Anthropological Museum
  • Marshall's backstory: illiterate miner → 8 years football → state legislator → prosecutor
  • Lost Haven corruption explained: relief check fraud, "dead souls" scheme
  • Henry warns of "dragons' eggs": young Pucas hatching
  • Henry recites Bagarthach curse: "Oh Mandrake man, of giants bred..."
  • Physical fight: Henry defeats Marshall but lets him live
  • Marshall leaves the lost fight still confident of other means of victory. [1968, p. 97]

Mandrake Marshall's Backstory

⚖
The Self-Made Monster

At seventeen: "a powerful boy, a complete illiterate" working in Stutgard's strip mines. Stutgard sponsored his education. Eight years of reading gave him "total recall": "There is very little about History or Philosophy or Philology or Economics or the Beautiful Letters that I do not know."

Made house whip in the state legislature by terrorizing fellow members. Became prosecutor. "I'm a woollier man than any masquerading ape."

The Puca Specimen in the Museum

Henry explains the museum prank: his dead kinsman had been displayed as Puca Man beyond Modern Man in the sequence. The claim to be last and highest makes the evolutionary joke an assertion of Puca supremacy. [1968, p. 91]

Dragons' Eggs

"You'll not become dominant here. We'll kill you off like the damned dragons you are."
"Yes, I begin to think that you will. But you won't win by it. We've laid dragons' eggs behind us. They're hatched and going now. You'll not know the young while they're growing. They are a time bomb in you."
[1968, p. 92]

Henry's Bagarthach Curse on Marshall

The Talking Rifle
Oh Mandrake man, of giants bred,
You didn't guess one singing trifle
Would ever enter in your head—
A message from a talking rifle.
— Henry Dulanty ☠ Prophetic Kill[1968, p. 95]

This verse will be fulfilled in Chapter 15 when Marshall is shot.

The Fight

It was, of course, a war of the Worlds.
— Narrator on Henry’s fight with Marshall [1968, p. 96]

Notable Quotations

"I like to come to the point. You're a dead man, Dulanty. Man, Hell! I consider you an animal, and I'll kill you for one."
— Marshall's opening
[1968, p. 91]
"There is enmity between our flesh from the beginning. We fought before, in an ice cave a million years ago, either on Earth or off it. You're an almost-man."
— Marshall to Henry
[1968, p. 94]
"Two worlds have met here this afternoon in our persons. Our talk seemed trivial, but it was key stuff. We could not strike a modus. Now we go to war, each world in its own fashion."
— Henry
[1968, p. 96]

Puca Lore

  • Homo Pucalis: Henry’s species-name joke, printed with a P. [1968, p. 91]
  • Neanderthal connection: Henry proposes that Pucas may have been the original Neanderthals; his statement is conjecture. [1968, p. 91]
  • Dominance imperative: "We are small in numbers even on our home world; there are never more than a few hundred of us on any world we control. It is therefore necessary that we become the dominant elite, or perish."
  • Fluidity: "We are the more fluid, and therefore we dominate. If we have to alter the world to our way, we will do it."
  • Bagarthach as weapon: Henry claims his Bagarthach can "milk a cow, charge a battery, or kill a man."
❧
Gogol and the Business of Lost Haven

Marshall’s Pavel Ivanovitch is Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov of Gogol’s Dead Souls. Chichikov buys dead serfs who are still on official lists and plans to use them as financial security. Stutgard adapts the principle to relief payments for dead, absent, and invented people. The falsified crop histories are a second fraud. [1968, pp. 94–95]

Sources: Gogol, Dead Souls, part 1, ch. 11.

❧
Marshall’s Learned Threats

Atropos is the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Marshall announces himself as Henry’s Atropos; Henry’s “oldest and ugliest” is an insult, not a standard ranking of the three Fates. “Beautiful Letters” renders belles-lettres. Against Marshall’s repertory of cultural knowledge, Henry answers with a verse that acts as a weapon. The subsequent “war of the Worlds” echoes the title of H. G. Wells’s novel. [1968, pp. 93–96]

❧
Dragon’s Teeth and Dragon’s Eggs

In the Cadmus story, sown dragon’s teeth produce armed men. Henry speaks instead of eggs that have hatched and are growing, and Witchy later calls the children her Dragons’ Seed. The classical story is a parallel for dangerous offspring; the novel changes teeth to eggs. [1968, pp. 92, 127, 144]

Sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3, Cadmus and the dragon’s teeth.

← Chapter 10 · Chapter 12 →

Chapter 12

A Mountainful of Murdered Indians

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 98–111]

Fulbert and a lawyer visit the children; evidence emerges that could save Henry.

Summary

Fulbert Fronsac brings a T-Town lawyer to the children's hiding place. Helen and Peter spot them from afar and taunt Fulbert: "You'll never get the Île back!" The lawyer seeks testimony about Stutgard's murder. Helen insists on protocol: "In the best society, one first speaks at length of everything else." She estimates Misu Mound contains thirty thousand murdered Indians and claims they've talked with some inside.

Dorothy’s fire and Helen’s shouted directions interrupt the visit. Helen later serves painfully hot tea to Fulbert and the lawyer and enjoys their mistake in taking the glasses. [1968, pp. 101–104]

The lawyer sees the children’s speech and lip movements come apart and catches strange shapes at the edge of his vision. Charles urges him to proceed with the questions while Helen is away. [1968, pp. 102–105]

The lawyer learns that John brought away Crocker’s large axe, marked with a C, and that Elizabeth hid it. Dorothy separately says Charles marched the missing boys into the woods, killed them, and cut off their ears. Fulbert dismisses her after the completed statement, not after an interruption. [1968, pp. 106–108]

The guard’s hint that Henry may soon be released is mistaken for a warning of lynchers. Henry prepares a noisy disturbance, then uses Frank’s key and his verse to escape at five minutes before nine in the evening. He leaves the jailer unconscious. [1968, pp. 109–111]

Key Events

  • Fulbert and unnamed T-Town lawyer arrive seeking testimony
  • Helen insists on social protocol; discusses Misu Mound's "thirty thousand murdered Indians"
  • Dorothy starts a fire heating water; Helen gives instructions via shouting
  • Helen serves scalding tea, burns the lawyer and Fulbert's hands
  • Lawyer notices telepathic speech, glimpses gargoyle shapes at vision's edge
  • Revelation: John took Crocker's bloody axe by mistake; Elizabeth hid it
  • Dorothy explicitly accuses Charles of killing the three missing boys; Fulbert dismisses her account. [1968, pp. 106–107]
  • Lawyer and Fulbert depart with the murder weapon
  • Henry misunderstands guard's hint: breaks out of jail thinking lynch mob coming

Misu Mound

▲
The Burial Mound

Helen estimates about thirty thousand occupants, invoking cubic capacity and centuries of settling. The figure is Helen’s own fanciful calculation. [1968, p. 100]

The mound represents the children's kinship with the displaced and murdered, another people destroyed by Earth's dominant culture. They have found "a hold more near their blood" among the dead Indians.

The Evidence

  • John's small axe was left at the scene (too small for the wounds)
  • Crocker's axe was taken by John: bloody, with Crocker's prints
  • The axe has "the big C burned into the haft"
  • Bad John witnessed Crocker kill Stutgard
  • Crocker dropped the axe when he saw Bad John (visible and transparent simultaneously)

The Lawyer's "Waking Dream"

The lawyer experiences something uncanny while with the children:

They think out loud when they wish to do so, and vocal cords (if such they have) have nothing to do with it.
— The lawyer’s waking dream, as narrated [1968, p. 102]

He also sees "a veritable gargoyle" in his peripheral vision: the children's true appearance glimpsed sideways.

Helen's Tea Ceremony

Helen insists on elaborate protocol: "In the best society, one first speaks at length of everything else except the subject directly on the mind." The lawyer and Fulbert are burned when Helen serves tea in glasses "so hot as to be almost incandescent": "I always wanted to find someone dumb enough to do that to."

Three Missing Boys

The lawyer asks about three missing boys. Dorothy says Charles marched them into the woods, killed them, and cut off their ears. Fulbert dismisses the accusation as fantasy after she completes it. The real ears and the narrator’s account of Peter’s silencer in Chapter 9 bear on her statement. [1968, pp. 79–81, 106–107]

Notable Quotations

"When I have left them, I always carry away the impression that it is they who are the real people, and that the real people are a little less."
— Fulbert Fronsac
[1968, p. 107]
You’ve just had a brush with a multiplex alien mind. You’ve hardly noticed the effect yet, but you’ll never be the same again.
— Fulbert to the lawyer [1968, p. 107]
❧
Burial History and Competing Claims

Spiro provides a regional comparison for the mound’s accumulated burials and the removal of its contents. Its major mound-building period was approximately 850–1450. Shawnee migration likewise involved several groups and routes. Helen’s and Phoebe’s accounts compete. [1968, pp. 100–103]

Sources: “Spiro Mounds,” Oklahoma Historical Society; “Shawnee Tribe (Loyal Shawnee),” Oklahoma Historical Society; “Shawnee, Absentee,” Oklahoma Historical Society.

❧
A Greek Poison and a Gothic Blade

Koneion is Greek for hemlock. The lawyer’s learned request becomes Helen’s poker-like exchange about Socrates, with Peter silently supplying the answer. Witchy’s later pendulum “like a scimitar” recalls the bladed pendulum in Poe’s “The Pit and the Pendulum.” The verbal resemblance is close; the novel does not name Poe. [1968, pp. 104, 108]

Sources: Poe, “The Pit and the Pendulum”.

← Chapter 11 · Chapter 13 →

The Unlikely Lock
Unlikely lock, unlucky lock,
I’ll batter you ka-zow ka-zammy
The way the chopper chopped the block,
And bust you with a mummy-whammy!
— Henry [1968, p. 109]

Antagonists

The Earth people who would destroy the Dulantys. By the novel's end, all the major antagonists are dead, killed by Bagarthach, by each other, or by Phoebe Jane's rifle.

Mandrake Marshall

Role: County Prosecutor Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 15

The self-made monster. Marshall is the novel's primary human villain, a former illiterate miner who educated himself into becoming a ruthless prosecutor. He orchestrates Henry's persecution, murders both Henry and Thomas Butterfield, and kills Frank before being shot by Phoebe Jane.

Backstory

At seventeen, Marshall was "a powerful boy, a complete illiterate" working in Stutgard's strip mines. Stutgard sponsored his education. Eight years of reading gave him "total recall": "There is very little about History or Philosophy or Philology or Economics or the Beautiful Letters that I do not know."

He became house whip in the state legislature "by terrorizing fellow members." As prosecutor, he intends to build his career on the "monster-kill": prosecuting Henry as an inhuman creature.

On the Dulantys

There is enmity between our flesh from the beginning. We fought before, in an ice cave a million years ago, either on Earth or off it. You’re an almost-man.
— Marshall to Henry [1968, p. 94]

Key Actions

  • Confronts Henry in jail: beaten in fight (Chapter 11)
  • Leads the manhunt for escaped Henry (Chapter 13)
  • Murders Henry at Butterfield's farm (Chapter 14)
  • Murders Thomas Butterfield as witness (Chapter 14)
  • Kills Frank from behind (Chapter 15)

Death

Shot by Phoebe Jane Lanyard while hunting Charles through the bogs. Henry's Bagarthach is fulfilled: "A message from a talking rifle." Charles rolls his body into the quicksand alongside Crocker and Frank.

"It's going to be getting a little bit crowded in that bog, and there aren't any of them very friendly to each other."
— Charles
[1968, p. 138]
— Charles, after rolling Marshall into the bog

Crocker

Role: Local Bully Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 15

The first to bark at the Dulantys. Crocker is the actual murderer of Coalfactor Stutgard, though Henry is blamed. He becomes the chief hound in Marshall's pack, tracking the Dulantys with his seven great dogs. Helen's Bagarthach curse follows him to his death.

Character

Crocker is described as a bully and a follower; he barks at the Dulantys on their arrival but serves Marshall's purposes. He kills Stutgard with an axe (witnessed by Bad John) and lets Henry take the blame. The rope Frank places around his neck haunts him until his death.

The Noose

Frank puts the noose around Crocker’s neck at Blind Ben’s Bar in Chapter 7. He orders him to wear it home, keep it handy, and await being sent for. Later it hangs from Crocker’s bedpost and torments him. [1968, pp. 63, 129–130]

The Seven Hounds

※
Crocker's Dogs

Mastiffs: Bell, Book, and Candle

Hounds: Luke, John, Barnabas, and Timothy

"Part mastiff and Great Pyrenees and part staghound." There is "an ancient antipathy between Pucas and every sort of dogs, but especially the great hounds."

Death

Frank catches Crocker and forces him into the quicksand with the noose around his neck. When Marshall kills Frank, Crocker sinks completely. Helen's verse is fulfilled: "On else than gallows be you hanged! / In else than water be you drownded!"

Coalfactor Stutgard

Role: Richest Man in Lost Haven Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 3

The man who sponsored Marshall. Stutgard is the richest man in Lost Haven, owner of the strip mines where Marshall once worked. He confronts the Dulantys on their arrival and is cursed by Peter. He is murdered by Crocker before the children can kill him.

Character

Stutgard’s power rests partly on fraud: relief checks for dead, departed, or fictitious residents, false crop histories, and payments connected with mined land. Marshall and Crocker have shared the proceeds; Marshall expects to inherit the operation. Crocker kills Stutgard; the novel does not fully explain his motive. [1968, pp. 94–95, 108]

Death

Killed by Crocker with an axe. Bad John witnesses the murder. Peter's Bagarthach is fulfilled: "Beware of jackals bearing axes!" The children arrive to kill him and find he's already dead.

Sheriff Train

Role: Local Sheriff Status: Alive

The lawman bullied by Marshall. Sheriff Train is the nominal law in Lost Haven but is completely dominated by Marshall. He arrests Henry with five deputies ("six shaking men") and participates in the manhunt, but is pushed aside by Marshall at every turn.

Character

Train is portrayed as weak rather than evil. He enforces the law as he understands it but lacks the will to stand against Marshall. When Marshall takes over the manhunt broadcast, Train can only protest feebly. He survives the novel.

You’re not going to talk to anybody alone. If you’re going to say anything, say it real fast right now, and then come along.
— Sheriff Train to Henry [1968, p. 33]

Thomas Butterfield

Role: Farmer Status: Deceased Death: Chapter 14

The man who trusted Marshall. Butterfield is a local farmer, "middling good, hard to scare, and a little stupid." He makes a citizen's arrest of Henry despite Henry's warnings that Marshall will kill them both.

Death

Marshall shoots Butterfield to eliminate the witness to Henry’s murder. Butterfield appeals to his former vote for Marshall; his confidence in the elected official is fatal. [1968, pp. 127–128]

Continue to: Allies & Others →

Chapter 13

In Brazen Clash of Helm and Greave

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 112–120]

Henry is already out of jail when Marshall arrives; the manhunt begins.

Summary

Marshall and Sheriff Train arrive after Henry’s escape. Marshall takes command of the broadcast, presents Henry as an armed killer, strikes Train when he raises the case against Crocker, and makes the jailer act near death. [1968, pp. 112–114]

Marshall picks up Crocker. They discuss their plans with relish. Marshall wants to shoot Henry multiple times in nonfatal areas: "I'll make him howl." Crocker wants his dogs to do the killing: "They had him half eaten before we got to him. They tore four- and six-pound hunks of meat right out of him... A man is mighty loud when you do that to him. I like a man to scream that way."

John Lewis Grew, called John Loose Screw, leads Henry to the Lost Moon Bar. The men recognize Pucas from inherited stories of help in establishing a system. Sammy Bluefield drives Henry through a roadblock in his modified car. The crash breaks Sammy’s collarbone; Henry continues on foot. [1968, pp. 116–120]

Key Events

  • Marshall arrives too late; Henry already escaped
  • Marshall strikes Sheriff Train, forces jailer to feign dying
  • Broadcasts lies: "Mad Killer" armed and dangerous
  • Marshall and Crocker discuss torture plans: shooting, dogs eating alive
  • Henry meets John Loose Screw in the woods, led to Lost Moon Bar
  • "Big Indians" recognize Henry from grandmother stories
  • Sammy Bluefield smashes roadblock at high speed; the car flips
  • Sammy breaks collarbone; Henry continues on foot
  • Next chapter: Henry reaches the Butterfield farm after escaping the roadblock. [1968, pp. 121–123]
  • Next chapter: Butterfield arrests Henry and telephones the authorities. [1968, pp. 123–124]

Characters Introduced

John Lewis Grew (John Loose Screw) Sammy Bluefield Thomas Butterfield

Henry's Escape

Previously, in Chapter 12: Frank’s key and Henry’s verse open the way out. Henry subdues the jailer and escapes at five minutes before nine in the evening. Chapter 13 opens with Marshall and Train arriving too late. [1968, pp. 109–112]

Marshall's Manhunt

Marshall takes control, ordering Sheriff Train around and threatening violence. He broadcasts lies: that Henry took the jailer's gun (he didn't), that he left the jailer "dying" (he's fine), that the "Mad Brother" Frank is also armed and dangerous.

"He'll keep coming after I put eight or nine shots into him, Crocker. I believe I can put them just where I want them. I'm the best shot in this country, and I know my anatomy."
[1968, p. 114]

Crocker's Dogs

※
The Seven Hounds

Mastiffs: Bell, Book, and Candle

Hounds: Luke, John, Barnabas, and Timothy

"They're part mastiff and Great Pyrenees and part staghound." Crocker reminisces about a previous escapee: "they had him half eaten before we got to him. They tore four- and six-pound hunks of meat right out of him."

The Indians' Aid

The Lost Moon Bar offers recognition through inherited stories and practical aid. John Loose Screw guides Henry; Sammy Bluefield risks the roadblock with him. [1968, pp. 116–120]

Sammy's car has "a chrome-plated dozer blade on the front... and a vertical slicer. It's the sportiest-looking front in the world, and it'll kindle any block."

Thomas Butterfield

Forward reference to Chapter 14. Butterfield arrests Henry and calls the authorities. He trusts Marshall despite Henry’s warning that the prosecutor will kill them both. [1968, pp. 123–128]

Notable Quotations

"There is an ancient antipathy between Pucas and every sort of dogs, but especially the great hounds."
[1968, p. 115]
"There is belief that the Indians had fast cars before the Flood. They remembered them more than did other people when mankind was reconstituted, and more than other people they know what to do with them."
[1968, p. 119]
❧
Henry’s Dark Wood

The sentence in which Henry comes to himself in a dark wood, with the straight way lost, closely follows the opening of Dante’s Inferno in the revised Carlyle translation. John Loose Screw becomes his local guide. [1968, pp. 115–117]

Sources: Dante, Inferno 1.1–3, Carlyle translation as revised.

❧
Law, Obligation, and a Date

The Lost Moon Bar’s “Pragmatic Sanction” and “Categorical Imperative” comically inflate a practical expectation that Henry will pay for the house. Sammy’s “Oklahoma State ’63” is a chronological clue: if read as his graduation year, the action cannot precede 1963. The university adopted the Oklahoma State name in 1957. [1968, pp. 117–120]

Sources: Oklahoma State University, 1957 name change.

❧
The Pack’s Names

Bell, Book, and Candle recall the old ritual of solemn excommunication. The hounds’ names extend the religious pattern through Luke, John, Barnabas, and Timothy; Matthew and Mark belong to earlier bloody encounters with a boar raccoon and a bear. The names give an ecclesiastical cast to a pack used for terror. [1968, pp. 114–115, 131]

Sources: John A. Hardon, “Bell-Book-Candle,” Modern Catholic Dictionary.

Chapter 14

Fit Subject For Heroic Chantey

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 121–128]

The murder of Henry Dulanty, fit subject for heroic chantey.

Summary

Henry selects a farmhouse by its dog ("a finely bred, strongly built, slightly stupid dog"), reasoning the master will be "middling good, hard to scare, and a little stupid." He enters the dark house and is blinded by Thomas Butterfield's flashlight. Butterfield holds a .45, demanding the jailer's gun. Henry has none: "If you believe I had a gun, then you believe it to your death."

Butterfield telephones the authorities. Henry asks him to have the sheriff contacted by telephone so Marshall and Crocker will not hear a broadcast. The message is nevertheless to be relayed by radio to whichever officer is nearest. Butterfield’s trust in that process defeats Henry’s attempt to control who arrives. [1968, pp. 124–125]

Marshall’s first shot strikes Henry high in the shoulder from behind. He shoots him again in the groin and gut while taunting him to rise. Crocker then shoots Henry in the face and kills him. The narration insists that Henry’s altered face in death is not less than human. [1968, pp. 126–127]

Butterfield finally realizes that he too will be killed. Marshall changes to the jailer’s handgun, laughs at Butterfield’s appeal, and shoots him. [1968, pp. 127–128]

Key Events

  • Marshall arrives before Henry can escape
  • Henry is shot multiple times while Marshall taunts him
  • Crocker delivers the killing shot to the face
  • Marshall kills Butterfield to eliminate the witness
  • Both deaths staged to blame Henry

Deaths

Night of Chapter 14
Henry Dulanty ☠ Murder by Marshall & Crocker
Shot repeatedly by Marshall in a prolonged killing. Final shot to the face by Crocker. "The Dulantys could manage to look like regular people, till they had to laugh, or die."
Minutes later
Thomas Butterfield ☠ Murder by Marshall
"I voted for you once," Butterfield says. Marshall laughs and shoots. Henry's prediction fulfilled: "If Marshall gets here first... He can't leave you alive to give testimony against him."

The Heroic Chantey

Throughout the chapter, Latin and English phrases appear as section breaks, fragments of a heroic verse about Henry's death:

Fragments in Narrative Order
On the Sands of Hesitation—
On the Sands of Hesitation—
Broached and Breached the Craft Dulanty—
Panged by Pygmies, Irked by Earthman—
He the Monster, by the Midgets—
On a Farmstead Near Catoosa—
In a Trap, Who’d Ambled Planets—
Finding Time Beshorn of Forelock—
De Profundis in Patinam—
Stewed in Stifling Introspection—
Stream of Thought—the Earthen Sickness—
Lost the Swiftness of the Puca—
Stranded Like a Fool, Dulanty—
On the Reefs of Earth—Untimely—
Passed the Final Fatal Moment—
Piger Tempus Edax Rerum—
Door of Time Against the Puca—
Ensorceled Earth—a Bomb Inside You—
Dragons’ Children Hatching, Growing—
Come the Green-Eyes, Come Requiting—
Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum.
— Chapter 14 [1968, pp. 122–127]

Marshall's Sadism

"Get up, Dulanty! A shot like that doesn't hurt a man like you! You've got a dozen more coming."
[1968, p. 126]
"Come on, Dulanty! One more time! Come get a piece of me—"
[1968, p. 127]

The Puca Face in Death

"Henry's shot face had become somewhat unhuman in repose, but not less than human. The Dulantys could manage to look like regular people, till they had to laugh, or die."
[1968, p. 127]

Notable Quotations

“You can’t kill me,” he said seriously. “I voted for you once.”
— Thomas Butterfield [1968, p. 128]
"One. And two. Marshall had had a good night. He looked at Crocker. Should he try for three?"
[1968, p. 128]
❧
A Frolic of His Own

The opening explanation Sammy might offer for the wreck uses a legal expression associated with acting outside the scope of one’s employment. Applied to his drive through the roadblock, it adds professional language to the aftermath. [1968, p. 121]

Sources: “Frolic and detour,” Cornell Legal Information Institute.

❧
The Chantey’s Falling Rhythm

The twenty-one verse fragments, including the repeated opening line, are built largely on a falling four-beat rhythm, like the trochaic tetrameter of Longfellow’s The Song of Hiawatha. The Latin phrases and other variations break the pattern. [1968, pp. 122–127]

Sources: Longfellow, The Song of Hiawatha.

❧
Hesitation, Thought, and Lost Time

“Sands of Hesitation” resembles the “Plains of Hesitation” maxim traced to George W. Cecil’s 1928 advertising copy. “Stream of Thought” is also the title of chapter 9 of William James’s The Principles of Psychology. Both phrases fit Henry’s disabled power of decision. Time without a forelock reverses the traditional figure of an opportunity that must be grasped as it approaches: once it passes, there is no hair behind to seize. Phaedrus’s “Tempus” is an ancient version of that figure. [1968, pp. 122–125]

Sources: “Chapter & Verse,” Harvard Magazine, July–August 2003; William James, The Principles of Psychology, ch. 9; Phaedrus, Fables 5.8, “Tempus”.

❧
The Three Latin Tags

De Profundis in Patinam, out of the depths into the dish or pan, combines the opening of Psalm 129 in the Vulgate numbering (130 in most modern Bibles) with the language of culinary peril. Tempus edax rerum, time the devourer of things, comes from Ovid; the printed Piger has masculine form where grammatical agreement with neuter tempus would require pigrum. Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum replaces the dead with monsters in the maxim forbidding ill speech of the dead. [1968, pp. 124–127]

Sources: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.234–36.

← Chapter 13 · Chapter 15 →

Chapter 15

The Battle Joined That Could But Leave

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 129–138]

The outre scene: Frank hunts Crocker; Marshall hunts Frank; Phoebe Jane watches them all.

Summary

Crocker cannot sleep, haunted by the transparent boy who watched him murder Stutgard, by Henry's dying words ("You haven't seen the last of me"), by the noose on his bedpost. At dawn he gathers his seven dogs, a rifle, a noose, and a bottle of "Spirits of Panther." He will kill the ghost child so he can sleep again.

From Misu Mound, Fulbert and an old dead Indian watch the drama unfold. The Indian counts the hunters: "Crocker hunts his prey. Another hunts Crocker. Another follows the man who follows Crocker. And a fourth hunter waits in ambush for the third." Fulbert has missed one person entirely.

Crocker follows Bad John into the bog. Barnabas departs, then the other three hounds, then Book and Bell; Candle stays. After dozing and dreaming of Stutgard, Crocker wakes with Frank’s noose around his neck. [1968, pp. 133–134]

Frank forces Crocker into the bog with the noose looped over a sycamore branch. "You killed Stutgard and, more important, you killed my brother." Crocker protests that Marshall killed Henry and he only watched. Before Frank can finish, Marshall arrives silently and strikes Frank from behind with a rifle butt: "one of the really colossal things." Crocker sinks into the quicksand as the rope slips from Frank's hand.

Marshall rolls Frank into the bog after striking him. Charles runs toward Marshall, firing; Marshall prepares to shoot the child. Phoebe Jane’s concealed shot kills Marshall. Charles thinks his own shot succeeded, examines the body, and rolls Marshall into the bog. [1968, pp. 135–138]

Key Events

  • Crocker sets out at dawn with seven dogs, rifle, noose, whiskey
  • Hunts Bad John through the bog; trail crosses impassable ground
  • Barnabas departs, followed by the other three hounds, then Book and Bell; Candle stays. [1968, pp. 133–134]
  • Crocker dreams of Stutgard attacking him; wakes with noose around neck
  • Frank forces Crocker into the bog at rope's end
  • Marshall kills Frank from behind with rifle butt
  • Crocker sinks into quicksand as rope slips
  • Charles arrives running, firing at Marshall
  • Phoebe Jane shoots Marshall from ambush: "a message from a talking rifle"
  • Marshall rolls Frank into the bog; Charles later rolls Marshall in. [1968, pp. 136–138]

Crocker's Dogs

※
The Seven Hounds

Mastiffs: Bell, Book, and Candle

Hounds: Luke, John, Barnabas, and Timothy

Matthew and Mark, the earlier dogs, belong to two separate bloody stories: one of a boar coon, one of a young fast bear. In the present hunt Barnabas leaves first, the other three hounds next, and Book and Bell after them. Candle stays and is claimed by Marshall. [1968, pp. 131, 133–136]

Deaths

The Outre Scene
Crocker ☠ Hanged/Drowned in Quicksand
Frank puts the noose around his neck and forces him into the bog. When Marshall kills Frank, Crocker sinks completely. Helen's verse fulfilled: "In else than water be you drownded!"
Moments later
Frank Dulanty ☠ Murdered by Marshall
"Marshall hit Frank Dulanty a terrific blow on the back of the head with his rifle butt. The blow was one of the really colossal things. He may have killed Frank with the one blow."
Moments later
Mandrake Marshall ☠ Shot by Phoebe Jane
Henry's Bagarthach fulfilled: "A message from a talking rifle." Shot by Phoebe Jane Lanyard while he hunts Charles. "She wasn't free from bloodlust herself. She'd never liked Marshall at all."

The Outre Scene

"Puca dramas differ in pace and climax from the dramas of Earth people. In the high classic form, there is always a scene (very near the end) where all the bloody stuff is heaped together for the greater enjoyment and convenience of all. It is extravagant and outré. It is both tragic and comic in the tall burlesque of it."
[1968, p. 133]

Crocker's Delirium

Before his death, Crocker is haunted by visions: Bad John (transparent and floating), the noose on his bedpost, dreams of Marshall coming to kill him. He hunts Bad John but cannot catch him: "He is quite a small boy... but not that small. He cannot be weightless."

Charles as Patriarch

Charles’s attempt to kill Marshall is earnest. He comes away believing he succeeded, although the narrator gives the effective shot to Phoebe Jane. [1968, pp. 136–139]

Fulbert's Observation

From atop Misu Mound, Fulbert watches the drama unfold with an old dead Indian. The Indian notes there are four hunters: Crocker hunting Bad John, Frank hunting Crocker, Marshall hunting Frank, and a fourth "waiting in ambush for the third", Phoebe Jane.

Notable Quotations

"It's going to be getting a little bit crowded in that bog, and there aren't any of them very friendly to each other."
— Charles, after rolling Marshall's body into the quicksand
[1968, p. 138]
— Charles, after rolling Marshall into the bog
"Did you know that Indians have an expression very like Pucas when they have just killed someone? It's near the same look."
[1968, p. 138]
❧
Belling the Cat, Completing the Riddle

Crocker’s end fulfills Helen’s conditions: a hanging away from a gallows and a drowning in something other than water. Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Vita Merlini has a comparable riddle fulfilled through a death involving a fall, a tree, and drowning. [1968, pp. 15, 63, 134–136]

Sources: Aesop, “Belling the Cat”; Geoffrey of Monmouth, Vita Merlini, trans. John Jay Parry.
