Chapter 16

Or Altered World or Dead Dulanty

Copy-text: [1968, pp. 139–144]

The children depart at moonrise; Witchy delivers her final charge; the Dragons' Seed is loosed upon the world.

Summary

Late that afternoon, Charles announces: "We will cast off at moonrise, or at another rising a few seconds later." He has matured in one afternoon. Elizabeth and Peter are first and second mates; Helen is navigator. "Charles was captain. He had matured in one afternoon. Elizabeth and Peter and Helen were showier, but Charles became the steady one."

They spend the afternoon "celebrating all the accumulated deaths", composing Bagarthach verses "with the very blood dripping out of them" and drinking choc beer until "tipsy as a lilt of larks." Then comes the peculiar rite: they shed their Earth names and assume their Puca identities. Elizabeth becomes Coisreacan-Dia; Charles becomes Laidir; Peter becomes Carraig; Dorothy becomes Feirin-De; Helen becomes Lochrann; John becomes Dia-Ta-Caomh; Bad John becomes Ionuin.

Bad John has been absent for hours when the children acknowledge his departure. After dark Phoebe promises to have Witchy nearby to join them as they cast off. The naming has already happened in the afternoon. [1968, pp. 139–140]

Charles watches the rising moon and another faint body from a high tree, then dives down and orders the departure and horn signal. Witchy steps aboard as the raft passes the mound. [1968, pp. 140–141]

Witchy arrives to give her parting admonition. Her charge shifts from killing everybody toward controlling and altering the world, though she still permits killing. After releasing her Dragons’ Seed she continues speaking, jokes about going to die, and takes the joke literally; Elizabeth answers her. [1968, pp. 141–144]

Six pairs of goblin eyes glowing green in the dark, and a seventh, older pair fading. "And opposed to them, only the defenseless World!"

Key Events

  • Charles announces departure at moonrise: "or at another rising"
  • Afternoon celebration: Bagarthach verses, choc beer until tipsy
  • Peculiar rite: children shed Earth names, assume Puca identities
  • Ionuin (Bad John) discovered missing: "gone for good"
  • Phoebe Jane delivers provisions: "Leave at moonrise"
  • Laidir Charles keeps moon-vigil, sees "another rising"
  • Charles orders the casting off and horn signal. [1968, p. 140]
  • Witchy boards the Île "as weightless as a ghost"
  • Witchy explains: Ionuin "gone with his father Frank"
  • Witchy's primitive ethic: "Be swift, and be sudden!"
  • The charge: "Break it."
  • "I break the egg! I turn you loose! Oh, my own Dragons' Seed!"
  • Witchy dies; six pairs of green eyes oppose the defenseless World

The Name Translations

✦
Puca Names Assumed
Elizabeth→Coisreacan-Dia
Charles→Laidir (strong)
Peter→Carraig (rock)
Dorothy→Feirin-De
Helen→Lochrann (beacon)
John→Dia-Ta-Caomh
Bad John→Ionuin (beloved)
Witchy→Briochtog (witch or sorceress)

Ionuin's Final Departure

When Helen asks about Bad John, Witchy explains: "Oh, he's gone with his father Frank. With us, small children are allowed to linger for a few years after they have died; but it isn't the custom on Earth. He was looking bad; I don't believe that the atmosphere here is very nourishing; now he'll be all right."

The River Journey

As they travel Green River, Witchy describes the way toward the Arkansas and Mississippi, then tangles the Nile with Little Egypt and Paducah. Helen challenges her geography. Witchy jokingly appeals to her recent classification as a filbert. [1968, p. 142]

Witchy predicts ten nights of moonlight. The departure releases a threat and a possibility into the world; the novel does not show what the children make of it. [1968, pp. 142–144]

Deaths

Night of departure
Witchy (Briochtog) ☠ Earth Allergy
"The Earth Sickness has caught me... I die tonight." She delivers her final charge and expires aboard the raft. "It's all right, Mama, go ahead and do it. Don't give it another thought."
Same night
Bad John (Ionuin): Departed
"I think that Ionuin Bad John has gone too... I believe he's gone for good." The ghost child's final passing is marked with another bloody Bagarthach verse.

Witchy's Final Charge

"There is on this world a most peculiar and remarkable ethic. The people of this world fail it by not taking it literally enough. Ourselves, if we try it, will fail it by taking it too literally."
[1968, p. 141]

She tells of a Puca cousin who followed the Earth ethic literally ("If your right hand offend you, hack it off") until "there was nothing left of him but the torso."

"Ourselves, we live by a more primitive ethic. We do not deny that it is primitive, but it is the only ethic that the Giver has given us yet. We live that primitive ethic all the way. Be swift, and be sudden! That is our secret."
[1968, p. 141]

Dragons' Seed

You know the banter line, ‘Do you really look like that, or you just kidding?’ Why, I’ve been kidding ever since I came to Earth. We all have been, to a degree. Let us all look like ourselves now and let the world be damned.
— Witchy, recalling a banter line [1968, pp. 142–143]
There isn’t any way to live in accord with this World as it is, children. You will have to chance it here and there, and sometimes you will have to excise elements that seem important to Earth people. It’s a stubborn and worthless old animal the way it is. Break it.
— Witchy; “chance” is the copy-text reading [1968, p. 143]
"I break the egg! I turn you loose! Oh, my own Dragons' Seed!"
[1968, p. 144]

The Final Image

Six little pair of goblin eyes glowing green in the dark; and a seventh older pair nictitated by death slumber to a fainter green.

And opposed to them, only the defenseless World!

END
[1968, p. 144]

Notable Quotations

"Kill them when you feel the need of it, of course; but mostly you will control and alter till you see if something cannot be made of the place."
[1968, p. 143]
And there’s another phrase they have—‘a plague of demons.’ You aren’t, but to them you will seem so.
— Witchy [1968, p. 144]
❧
The Sermon on the Mount in Puca Speech

Witchy’s mutilated cousin acts out Matthew 5:29–30 with disastrous literalism. Her later “Salt of the Earth” is also from Matthew 5, verse 13. She finds the Earth ethic both remarkable and difficult, yet borrows its language for her own charge, and her advice to break the world runs against the Gospel phrase. [1968, pp. 141, 143]

Sources: Matthew 5:13, 29–30, Douay-Rheims.

❧
Little Egypt and the Last Earth Phrases

Little Egypt is a real regional name for southern Illinois. The Ohio meets the Mississippi at Cairo; Paducah is farther up the Ohio. Witchy’s Nile turns the regional nickname into comic geography. Her final “Dragons’ Seed” recalls the classical image of dragon’s teeth becoming armed men, while Dragon Seed is also Pearl S. Buck’s novel title. “A plague of demons” was the title of Keith Laumer’s 1965 Berkley novel. [1968, pp. 142–144]

Sources: Alexander County, Illinois, history and geography; SFWA, A Plague of Demons (1965).

← Chapter 15 · Return to Introduction

Allies & Others

The few who showed kindness to the Puca strangers, and the minor characters who populate Lost Haven and the strip pits.

❧
On Puca and "Interesting" Humans

The Dulantys find allies among people outside Lost Haven’s established power: Fulbert, Phoebe Jane, and the Indigenous men at the Lost Moon Bar. [1968, pp. 35, 47–48, 116–119]

Fulbert Fronsac

Role: Town Drunk / Lost Dauphin Status: Alive

The town drunk who is also the lost Dauphin. Fulbert is "an old French bum who was also the lost Dauphin. And, if not he, then he was the son of the Dauphin, or the grandson, sometimes the one, sometimes the other." He gives the children the Île de France and Catherine de Medici.

Character

Fulbert is one of the few who can see Bad John, whom he calls "Ange-Jacques." He represents the dispossessed royalty of an older world, French nobility reduced to Oklahoma vagrancy. He keeps his dignity and his claim to royal blood.

Key Actions

  • Gives the children the Île de France (Chapter 4)
  • Provides Catherine de Medici (Chapter 4)
  • Brings the lawyer to the children (Chapter 12)
  • Watches the outre scene from Misu Mound (Chapter 15)

On the Dulantys

"When I have left them, I always carry away the impression that it is they who are the real people, and that the real people are a little less."
[1968, p. 107]

Phoebe Jane Lanyard

Role: Strip Pit Resident / Ally Status: Alive

The Shawnee woman who saves the children and kills Marshall. Phoebe Jane runs Lanyard Landing in the strip pits. She's the only kingdom ruler the children cannot bring themselves to attack: "It is hard to plunder a people who will willingly give you anything they have."

Heritage

Phoebe Jane claims many grandfathers: Jean Chouteau, Charles Goodnight, Jesse Chisholm, both Jesse and Frank James, Charles Curtis, Chief Crazy Horse, David Payne, and Sequoyah. "The reason she had so many grandfathers was that she came from a big family."

She's "more Indian than the rest of her family" and has "a way of looking at the Dulantys and chuckling." She can "be as goblin as they could."

Key Actions

  • Trades provisions for the captured whisky (Chapter 6). [1968, pp. 47–48]
  • Brings supplies and news nightly (Chapter 6)
  • Promises to watch over the family (Chapter 6)
  • Pilots them to a better hiding spot (Chapter 6)
  • Shoots Marshall dead (Chapter 15)

On Finding the Children

"How could you find us when even the Fabers couldn't?"
"Oh, they're only Cherokees. I wonder God doesn't take their eyes away from them since they never use them."
[1968, p. 55]

Her Farewell

"It's so dark here that you didn't see me go, and I left my voice here to talk with you for two minutes after I'm gone."
[1968, p. 56]

The Killing of Marshall

Charles fires at Marshall and believes he has killed him. The narrator identifies Phoebe Jane’s effective rifle shot, whose calibre differs from Charles’s weapon. [1968, pp. 136–138]

Catherine de Medici

Role: She-Goat of Royal Blood Status: Alive

A she-goat of royal blood. The narrator gives Catherine de Medici her royal ancestry in the novel’s tall-tale register. Catherine travels with the children under the deed’s guest provisions. [1968, pp. 36–38]

Legal Status

Helen added clauses to the Île de France deed specifying Catherine's "guest status" and "disembarkation rights." The goat stays with the children aboard the raft.

Pandemonium John

Role: Traveling Puca Musician Status: Alive

The aged Puca musician. Pandemonium John travels with an elaborate wheeled apparatus. The forty or fifty instruments belong to the smaller machine he proposes for Charles. [1968, pp. 82–89]

Character

John has worked a nine-state circuit for decades, which makes the timetable of fatal Earth Allergy uncertain. He brings news of the parents, leads the honkeroo, and encourages Charles to build a smaller seagoing pandemonium with Peter’s mechanical help. [1968, pp. 86–90]

"There are towns in my nine-state area that haven't heard the shrill of my pandemonium for twenty years. There are fair-sized hamlets that I never have been run out of."
[1968, p. 89]

Little Jack Wilson

Role: Poor Man of Lost Haven Status: Alive

The man who warns Frank. Little Jack is a poor man of Lost Haven, summoned by Frank's Bagarthach to warn him of the planned lynching. He likes the Dulantys despite being scared of them.

"I like you and your kindred better than I like anyone else in town. You've treated me decently and made me feel like a person, but I'm the butt of the lowest Lost Haven clown of them all."
[1968, p. 57]

The Five Kingdoms

The Stinkers

Leaders: Elwood Elgin, Rex Remagen, Berny Bottleby

Three older boys (Elwood is 11) who rule "Port Stinker." Defeated in naval battle by the Dulantys. Their shack is burned, their raft (the Sea Bear) captured, and they are "drowned" but reach shallow water.

Amada Stutgard

Age: 10 Daughter of Coalfactor

Coalfactor Stutgard's daughter, now orphaned. Peter is sent to kill her but she gives her word to walk into the quicksand, then breaks it and escapes. "Earth people will lie to save their lives."

Jack Fiddler

Role: Whisky Maker (part Quapaw)

Jack Fiddler makes whisky and choc beer. Peter first holds him with the captured .22; Charles takes the larger rifle. Fiddler escapes, and the children fail to find his reserve stock and house. [1968, pp. 45–46]

The Fabers

Role: Commercial Fishermen (part Cherokee)

The Fabers run commercial fishing operations and are rumored to be "not above killing a stray child who came their way and chopping him up for bait." Their stronghold is destroyed but they escape and continue hunting the children.

Indian Allies

John Loose Screw

Nation: Quapaw

Guides Henry at the Lost Moon Bar during his escape. The Indians were told the Puca "would be along" to help set up a system; their information was "centuries out of date," but they still feel kinship.

Sammy Bluefield

Role: Driver

A young Indian with an incredibly fast car featuring "a chrome-plated dozer blade on the front... and a vertical slicer." He drives Henry through a roadblock at high speed. The car crashes but Sammy survives.

"There is belief that the Indians had fast cars before the Flood. They remembered them more than did other people when mankind was reconstituted."
[1968, p. 119]

Continue to: Gazetteer →

Lost Haven

Lost Haven is so shabby and overgrown that the arriving Dulantys fail to recognize the town. [1968, p. 15]

❦
The Hidden Town

The novel places Lost Haven in Oklahoma’s Rogers County country. On arrival, the Dulantys stop in what seems a weed patch and discover that they are already in the town. [1968, pp. 15–16]

The Big Shanty

Type: Residence Owner: Indian lady in Catoosa

The Dulanty home. A large, dilapidated structure built over old railroad tracks. The children tell their Aorach stories here in Chapter 1. Dorothy's ghost story references an old track running beneath the shanty where a ghost train passes.

Features

  • Built over abandoned railroad tracks
  • Houses four adults and six living children, with Bad John also present. [1968, pp. 12–15]
  • Rented from an Indian lady in Catoosa
  • Threatened during the planned lynching described in Chapter 7. [1968, pp. 57–63]
  • Dorothy's Bagarthach to burn it fails (Chapter 3)

The Two Jails

Type: County Facility

Lost Haven jail is the flimsy tin structure where Fulbert is held and the children enter through the roof. The county-seat jail is the stronger building to which Henry is taken. [1968, pp. 33, 35]

Key Events

  • Lost Haven jail: the children visit Fulbert and obtain the raft deed (Chapter 4). [1968, pp. 35–39]
  • County-seat jail: Henry is held for Stutgard’s murder (Chapter 4). [1968, p. 33]
  • County-seat jail: Marshall confronts Henry (Chapter 11). [1968, pp. 91–97]
  • County-seat jail: Henry escapes in the evening (Chapter 12). [1968, pp. 109–111]

Lost Moon Bar

Type: Tavern Clientele: Indian

Henry finds refuge at the Lost Moon Bar. The men there recognize his kind from grandmother stories, then provide help through John Loose Screw and Sammy Bluefield. [1968, pp. 116–120]

"There is belief that the Indians had fast cars before the Flood. They remembered them more than did other people when mankind was reconstituted, and more than other people they know what to do with them."
[1968, p. 119]

Stutgard House

Type: Residence Owner: Coalfactor Stutgard

Where Stutgard is murdered. The home of Lost Haven's richest man. John climbs through the window intending to kill Stutgard but finds him already dead, killed by Crocker. Bad John witnesses the murder and terrifies Crocker into dropping his axe.

Butterfield Farm

Type: Farm Location: Near Catoosa

Where Henry and Butterfield die. Thomas Butterfield's farm, where Henry attempts to hide after his escape. Butterfield makes a citizen's arrest and calls the authorities. Marshall arrives first and murders them both.

The Murders

Marshall shoots Henry in the shoulder from behind, then in the groin and gut. Crocker fires the fatal shot into Henry’s face. Marshall then kills Butterfield and arranges to blame Henry for the farmer’s death. [1968, pp. 126–128]

The Hospital / Asylum

Type: Medical Facility

Where Witchy is taken. After Witchy goes mad following Veronica's death, she is hospitalized. Phoebe Jane visits her "for a little while" and reports that "things look bad." Witchy escapes to deliver her final charge to the children in Chapter 16.

❧
Vinita and Wan-Wit

Vinita’s Eastern State Hospital received its first patients in 1913. It is the historical setting for the institution where Witchy is confined. Marshall’s “Wan-Wit on the Neosho” is his mocking name for it. [1968, pp. 64, 108, 114]

Sources: “Vinita,” Oklahoma Historical Society.

Continue to: The Strip Pits →

The Strip Pits

"A dozen square miles of mountains turned inside out, threaded by canals, and with bottomless chasms", the children's domain and battlefield.

⚒
Geography

The strip pits are the remnants of surface coal mining, vast excavations that have filled with water, creating a maze of canals, lakes, and artificial mountains of overburden. The landscape reminds the Puca of their home world, with its "land and water inextricably mixed."

The five kingdoms are encountered across Chapters 5 and 6: the Stinkers, Stutgard Landing, and Fiddler first; Lanyard Landing and the Fabers afterward. The children’s campaign includes attempted killing and destruction as well as alliance. [1968, pp. 40–56]

The Waterways

Green River

Type: Major Waterway

Green River is part of the novel’s water route toward the sea. The children spend their first night at sea there, and Helen tells her pirate saga. The novel gives it as narrative geography, not a surveyed route. [1968, pp. 30, 51–54]

The Canal System

A maze of interconnected waterways created by strip mining. The children navigate these in the Île de France, using the complexity to evade pursuit. Key features include:

  • Hidden inlets and mooring spots
  • Connections between different pit lakes
  • Shallow areas and quicksand bogs
  • The "bottomless chasms" of the deepest excavations

The Quicksand Bogs

Type: Hazard

The quicksand is both a threat and the site of the final deaths. Crocker sinks when Marshall’s blow makes Frank release the rope. Marshall rolls Frank in; Charles subsequently rolls Marshall in. [1968, pp. 134–138]

"It's going to be getting a little bit crowded in that bog, and there aren't any of them very friendly to each other."
— Charles
[1968, p. 138]
— Charles, after rolling Marshall into the bog

The Five Kingdoms

1. Port Stinker (Kingdom of the Stinkers)

Rulers: Elwood Elgin (11), Rex Remagen, Berny Bottleby Status: Conquered

First to fall. Three older boys rule this domain. The Dulantys attack in a naval battle, using Helen's Greek fire (burning paper sacks filled with glass, thumbtacks, cockleburs, and cactus). The children capture the Sea Bear and a .22 rifle. The Stinkers are "drowned" but reach shallow water.

Spoils

  • The Sea Bear (raft)
  • .22 rifle
  • Territory cursed with salt

2. Stutgard Landing

Ruler: Amada Stutgard (10) Status: Destroyed

Nearly abandoned after Coalfactor's death. The strip pit outpost of the Stutgard family. The shack is burned. Peter is sent to kill Amada, but she gives her word to walk to the quicksand, then breaks it and escapes.

"Earth people will lie to save their lives."
[1968, p. 44]

3. Fiddler's Landing

Ruler: Jack Fiddler (part Quapaw) Status: Raided

Fiddler’s domain yields whisky, choc beer, and weapons. Peter first covers Fiddler with the .22; Charles then takes the larger rifle. Fiddler escapes. [1968, pp. 45–46]

Spoils

  • Barrel of corn whisky
  • Barrel of choc beer
  • Tub of mash
  • A ham

Note: Fiddler's main reserve stock and house are never found.

4. Lanyard Landing

Ruler: Phoebe Jane Lanyard (part Shawnee) Status: Allied

The kingdom of kindness. The children cannot bring themselves to attack Lanyard Landing. "It is hard to plunder a people who will willingly give you anything they have." Phoebe Jane barters for the captured whisky and becomes the children's primary ally.

Trade Received

  • Pecans
  • Grape juice
  • Hominy grits
  • News of the family
  • Ongoing supply runs

5. Faber Stronghold

Rulers: The Fabers (part Cherokee) Status: Destroyed

The fishermen rumored to use children for bait. Commercial fishermen with a sinister reputation: "not above killing a stray child who came their way and chopping him up for bait." The children destroy their shack and boat, release hundreds of pounds of fish, and slash their nets.

Spoils

  • Two trotlines
  • Fish knives

The Fabers return to find ruin and continue hunting the children throughout the novel.

Misu Mound

Type: Burial Mound Contents: ~1,000 murdered Indians

Helen estimates about thirty thousand dead in Misu Mound. The number is her own calculation, not a census. The mound's layers and disputed accounts reach across different peoples, creatures, and ages. [1968, pp. 66–69, 100]

Significance

The mound gives the children a place of kinship among the Indigenous dead. The novel also gives competing stories of the mound, and the Puca have ambitions to rule. In Chapter 15, Helen trades a buffalo thighbone for an old dead woman’s own bone, which she wants for an artifact. [1968, pp. 66–69, 92, 100, 132–133]

Fulbert and an old dead Indian watch the outre scene from atop Misu Mound. Helen claims to have talked to old dead Indians inside the mound.

They Found a Hold More Near Their Blood
A Mountainful of Murdered Indians
— Chapter titles 11–12 [1968, pp. 91, 98]
❧
A Regional Setting

Catoosa, Rogers County, and Vinita locate the novel in northeastern Oklahoma. Rogers County’s coal was worked by strip mining. Source notes propose Green River/Verdigris and Crow Creek/Bird Creek correspondences; Bird Creek does meet the Verdigris near Catoosa, but the novel gives no exact map. Lost Haven and Misu Mound are fictional locations with no identified models. [1968, pp. 15, 30, 40, 58, 64]

Sources: “Rogers County,” Oklahoma Historical Society; USGS, Bird Creek locality at its Verdigris confluence; “Vinita,” Oklahoma Historical Society.

Continue to: Vessels →

Vessels

The Dulanty navy: rafts, captured craft, and the flagship Île de France.

Île de France

Type: Fishing Raft Former Owner: Fulbert Fronsac Status: Flagship

The Dulanty flagship. Fulbert’s fishing raft, with its boathouse and equipment, is exchanged for a stolen bottle of whisky. The grand French name suits Fulbert’s royal pretensions; a possible allusion to the ocean liner is unconfirmed. [1968, pp. 35–39]

Acquisition

The children visit Fulbert in jail and negotiate for the raft. Peter writes the deed; Helen adds amendments regarding Catherine de Medici's guest status. See Chapter 4.

The Deed

“To whomever it is respected,” Peter wrote slowly in a solemn voice after taking the paper and pencil. “This is to convey one raft the Île de France with the boathouse and blanket and lantern and automobile horn and the box of snuff and the frying pan and the coffee pot and other accessories in fee simple for one bottle of whisky stolen by Helen and John Dulanty and given in token to Fulbert Fronsac, dated today (I don’t know the date and I bet nobody else does either) and agreeable to all parties.”
— Narrator and Peter’s deed [1968, p. 38]

Equipment & Accessories

  • Boathouse (cabin structure)
  • Blanket
  • Lantern
  • Automobile horn
  • Box of snuff
  • Frying pan
  • Coffee pot
  • Catherine de Medici (she-goat, with guest rights)

Role in the Novel

The Île de France is the children's home, transport, and base of operations throughout their strip pit campaign. They sleep aboard, cook aboard, and flee aboard. In the final chapter, they cast off at moonrise to "be gone forever," with Witchy boarding to deliver her final charge before dying.

Crew Positions

  • Navigator: Helen
  • Mechanic: Peter (with Charles)
  • Cook: Dorothy (in training; prone to fires)
  • Lookout: Bad John

Sea Bear

Type: Raft Former Owner: The Stinkers Status: Captured

Prize of the Battle of Port Stinker. The Stinkers' raft, captured during the naval battle in Chapter 5. Towed behind the Île de France as a secondary vessel.

Capture

The Sea Bear is taken after the children defeat the Stinkers with Helen's Greek fire bombs. The three Stinker boys are "drowned" (they reach shallow water) and their territory salted. Along with the Sea Bear, the children capture a .22 rifle.

Jack Fiddler's Boat

Type: Unknown Status: Sunk

Jack Fiddler's vessel, sunk during the raid on Fiddler's Landing. Not captured; destroyed to deny the whisky maker transport.

The Faber Boat

Type: Fishing Vessel Status: Burned

The Fabers' commercial fishing boat, burned during the raid on their stronghold. The destruction of their vessel, along with their nets and stored fish, is a major economic blow to the Faber operation.

The Ghost Ships (Helen's Account)

In Chapter 6, Helen describes visits to three pirate ships on Green River and briefly names a fourth, the Flying Snake:

The Spanish Dancer

"It has the blankest pirates of all on it, except for the Flying Snake." Helen claims they made her captain after recognizing her worth.

The Vampire

"Whose crewmen are served every night a cup of blood with their scuttle of rum." They tested Peter's blood but released him when they discovered he was Puca: "We can't be drinking Puca blood; we got a contract with them."

The Gigantis Transfixus

In Helen’s saga, the giant has been spiked as the ship’s mast for thirty years. The term has already expired; an old calendar has deceived him. Helen says she frees him and survives the destruction. [1968, pp. 52–54]

The other children are skeptical of Helen's accounts. "Pirates are perhaps the greatest invention of Earth people," Elizabeth says loftily.

❧
A Fourth Name in Helen’s Account

Alongside the three ships described here, Helen briefly names the Flying Snake, whose pirates she calls still bloodier. Her account therefore names four ships, although only three receive extended attention. [1968, pp. 52–54]

Continue to: Puca Lore →

Bagarthach Verses

The printed four-line verses, followed by the interleaved Heroic Chantey. The separate chapter-title poem is available in the overview.

✦Power and Its Limits

Irish bagarthach / bagrach suggests threatening or menacing. The novel’s art is broader: curses, summons, taunts, songs, and an unlocking verse. Frank credits a counterverse with defeating Dorothy; Helen says verses often fail in dreams. The curses on Crocker and Stutgard precede their deaths by about six weeks; Henry’s curse is later.

[1968, pp. 8–9, 15–19, 30, 35, 95, 109]
The Wife’s Careless Verse
I’m turning livid in this bog,
This woolly world that spooks and spites you.
You’ll find that picture’s got a dog!
I hope the blinking bugger bites you!
— Within Elizabeth’s story [1968, p. 8]
Silly Jimmy Jelly
The engine spattered him like tar,
And broke his bones and burst his belly.
We gathered Jimmy in a jar.
Hey, pass the Silly Jimmy Jelly!
— Within Helen’s story [1968, p. 11]
Helen’s Curse on Crocker
Old Crocker man, be belled and banged!
You hound-dog hunk, we’ll have you hounded!
On else than gallows be you hanged!
In else than water be you drownded!
— Helen [1968, p. 15]
Peter’s Curse on Stutgard
Too long, too late you steal and strut;
Your bubble breaks, your grip relaxes!
Beware the under-studding, Stut!
Beware of jackals bearing axes!
— Peter [1968, p. 16]
The Crow
I catch you, crow, in curving orb
No matter how you caw and cough you!
I sing the corbie to the corb!
I sing the silly wings right off you!
— Helen [1968, p. 23]
Dorothy’s Attempt on the Adults
We’ll wither Witchy with a prank,
And kindle them in flames like roses—
Veronica and Hank and Frank—
And give them all Apotheosis.
— Dorothy [1968, p. 24]
Helen’s Dream-Verse
I blast you corny country cops,
I’ll blow the bars and locks, by hokey!
I’ll kill the sheriff’s cows and crops,
And get my papa out of pokey.
— Helen, within her story [1968, p. 30]
The Stinkers
Oh Stinker limbs that reek and rot,
Stinker head that decomposes!
We’ll splatter all the blood you’ve got,
You seven-letter sos-and-soses!
— Helen [1968, p. 41]
Witchy’s First Verse
The Devil and Crocker and Stut
Put all of their heads in one hat,
And mixed them and added them up,
And hadn’t the brains of a cat.
— Witchy at Vinita [1968, p. 64]
Witchy’s Second Verse
The Devil sent Crocker for Stut
To bring him his head on a plate.
The Devil said ‘I’m in a rut,
That’s something I oughtn’t to ate.’
— Witchy at Vinita [1968, p. 64]
Witchy’s Third Verse
The Devil rolled Stut like a ball
And said as he dropped in a hole,
‘It tickles my tail to recall
The prices he charged us for coal.’
— Witchy at Vinita [1968, p. 65]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 1
I had a wife I loved galore,
My blessed, brindled, blond Cobina,
Until my flute went out the door,
And out of bed my concertina.
— Pandemonium John [1968, pp. 82–83]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 2
I played the fiddle and the fife,
The harpsichord and hootie-hoosic,
But bled inside to hear my wife:
‘It’s loud enough, but is it music?’
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 83]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 3
I had a cow, I had a calf,
I had a pig, I had a pony.
I killed them all when they did laugh
And called my carols caco-phony.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 83]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 4
My daughter was my pride of life,
But at my tunes she was a scoffer.
I took the blinking butcher knife
And sheared the erring ears right off her.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 83]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 5
I had a dog who when I played
He cringed himself and whined and howled him.
I went for him with spit and spade
And cut him up and disembow’led him.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 84]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 6
I showered riches on my wife
And lived myself in durance frugal;
But she’d a fault that cost her life:
She chattered while I played the bugle.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 84]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 7
My daughter never lived to wed
For all my songs she’d sore berate them.
I cut the eyeballs from her head
And marinated them and ate them.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 84]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 8
I had a child, I had a wife,
I gave them all the pleasures due them;
Until one night with knout and knife
I fell upon them both and slew them.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 85]
Pandemonium’s Arrival · 9
No longer am I dim of brow,
No longer am I wan and harried,
Nor even critics irk me now,
They all of them are dead and buried.
— Pandemonium John [1968, p. 85]
The Advertisement
I’ll play the horn all night and day,
I’ll play the drum around your city.
The only time I’ll go away
Is when there’s money in my kitty.
— Sign on the pandemonium [1968, p. 88]
Elizabeth’s Verse About Helen
I had a little sister dear
As pretty as a springtime crocus.
I buried her without a tear,
She was a little too pre-co-cus.
— Elizabeth [1968, p. 90]
Helen’s Verse About Elizabeth
I also had a sister sweet,
I worshiped her, I idolized her,
Until I put her on to heat,
And accidentally vaporized her.
— Helen [1968, p. 90]
Henry’s Curse on Marshall
Oh Mandrake man, of giants bred,
You didn’t guess one singing trifle
Would ever enter in your head—
A message from a talking rifle.
— Henry [1968, p. 95]
The Unlikely Lock
Unlikely lock, unlucky lock,
I’ll batter you ka-zow ka-zammy
The way the chopper chopped the block,
And bust you with a mummy-whammy!
— Henry [1968, p. 109]

The Heroic Chantey

The fragments occur between passages of prose. The opening line appears twice and is retained twice here.

Fragments in Narrative Order
On the Sands of Hesitation—
On the Sands of Hesitation—
Broached and Breached the Craft Dulanty—
Panged by Pygmies, Irked by Earthman—
He the Monster, by the Midgets—
On a Farmstead Near Catoosa—
In a Trap, Who’d Ambled Planets—
Finding Time Beshorn of Forelock—
De Profundis in Patinam—
Stewed in Stifling Introspection—
Stream of Thought—the Earthen Sickness—
Lost the Swiftness of the Puca—
Stranded Like a Fool, Dulanty—
On the Reefs of Earth—Untimely—
Passed the Final Fatal Moment—
Piger Tempus Edax Rerum—
Door of Time Against the Puca—
Ensorceled Earth—a Bomb Inside You—
Dragons’ Children Hatching, Growing—
Come the Green-Eyes, Come Requiting—
Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum.
— Chapter 14 [1968, pp. 122–127]
✦Verses Mentioned but Not Transcribed

The novel refers to other Bagarthachs without giving their words, including Frank’s summons to Little Jack, counterverses, messages, and the children’s death celebrations.

[1968, pp. 35, 57, 86–87, 139–140]

Aorach Stories

"It was their way of defying that tricky place Earth... They whistled in the dark."

❡
On the Aorach

Aorach is a Puca narrative art, including ghost stories, accounts of family origins, and other kinds of tale. Irish aorach means satirical; aerach, a separate word used near the ending, can mean airy or lively. [1968, pp. 14, 18–19, 138]

"Listen, people, creatures, devices, entities, it was the meanest world in all the universes! It'd have spooked you too."

The Chapter 1 Stories

In Chapter 1, each of the six living children tells an Aorach story. Bad John cannot tell proper ghost stories: "he could only tell people stories, and nobody cares about them."

Elizabeth's Story: The Haunted Picture

▣
Theme: Careless Magic

Albert and his unnamed wife have a picture in which the man’s appearance changes. A dog then appears in it. [1968, pp. 7–9]

Frustrated with her husband, she makes a careless Bagarthach verse:

I'm turning livid in this bog,
This woolly world that spooks and spites you.
You'll find that picture's got a dog!
I hope the blinking bugger bites you!
[1968, p. 8]

The dog bites and kills the husband.

Moral: "Earth things are so dumb that they don't know when to obey a Bagarthach and when not to."

Charles's Story: The Country Hotel

⌂
Theme: Identity Dissolution

A Puca traveling salesman discovers Earth has been added to his territory. At a country hotel, strange things happen: a loud bang, lights turning on by themselves.

The tale’s shifting identities resolve into the hotel man’s corpse. The traveler escapes with a doorknob that becomes a rock, while the hotel disappears. [1968, pp. 9–10]

Theme: The instability of Earth reality; the impossibility of knowing what is real.

Helen's Story: Silly Jimmy

⚙
Theme: The Dead Who Don't Know

A man returns to his hometown and talks to Silly Jimmy by the railroad tracks. His family reminds him that Silly Jimmy died long ago, run over by a train. A mocking verse was made about him:

The engine spattered him like tar,
And broke his bones and burst his belly.
We gathered Jimmy in a jar.
Hey, pass the Silly Jimmy Jelly!
[1968, p. 11]

Yet fresh wood shavings prove Jimmy had been whittling, dead or not.

Theme: The persistence of the dead.

Peter's Story: Alice and Clarissa

❡
Theme: Trickery and Substitution

A girl named Alice dies and goes to Hell for stealing money, but it was really her sister Clarissa who did it. Alice returns as a ghost to scare Clarissa into confessing.

Clarissa takes Alice’s ghost sheet. The guard mistakes her for Alice and carries Clarissa to Hell, leaving Alice on Earth. [1968, pp. 11–12]

Moral: "A lot of times, you can make everything work all right if you send just one person out of a bunch to Hell."

Dorothy's Story: The Ghost Train

⚙
Theme: Haunted Ground

A man killed by a train returns once a year to swing a lantern on the tracks. One night he steals a real lantern, and a ghost train, the same one that killed him, switches onto the old track.

Dorothy says she makes a sign and the train passes through the shanty without breaking it up. It is not diverted away. [1968, p. 13]

Theme: The Big Shanty itself is haunted ground; the children live over a ghost railroad.

John's Story: William and Polly

†
Theme: The Promise Kept

A Puca man (William) and Earth woman (Polly) marry and promise that whoever dies first will return to tell the other what death is like. William dies; Polly remarries Tom.

William comes three times to the door:

  • First time: "It's cold."
  • Second time: "It's dark."
  • Third time: "It's lonesome."

Polly explains the first visits away as those of the coal man and kerosene man, then rejects William’s news of loneliness. A wind kills Tom, freezes Polly, destroys the house, and buries her. The tale ends with William’s claim to be showing her what death is like. [1968, pp. 13–14]

Theme: Promises to the dead cannot be escaped.

Bad John's Problem

He couldn’t tell ghost stories, he could only tell people stories, and nobody cares about them.
— Narrator on Bad John [1968, p. 14]

As a ghost himself, Bad John cannot tell proper ghost stories; he lacks the necessary distance from the subject. His "people stories" are dismissed by the other children.

The Parabolic Stories (Chapter 3)

In Chapter 3, four children tell stories while drying on tree branches after swimming. These are not traditional Aorach but parabolic accounts of recent traumas, told in oblique third person.

Elizabeth's Story: The Floozy

A thinly veiled account of finding Witchy gone mad. A little girl follows her mother's perfume through dark streets and finds "a crazy floozy." The floozy turns and says "My God, Elizabeth! That you should see me like this."

Reality: Elizabeth discovered Witchy's madness the night before.

Peter's Story: The Brown Bottle

A boy watches his father drink from a brown bottle. With each glass, the father changes: "like the man in the story that changed into a frog." His eyes go gray and glazed, his face reddens.

Connection: Peter’s story responds to Frank’s drinking and frightening transformation after Veronica’s death. [1968, pp. 27–28]

John's Story: The Onion and the Crate

A boy and his mother have only one onion to eat, eating one layer each night. When it's gone, the mother dies. The boy brings another onion, but she's been put in a crate. Her cold-iron grip catches his hand. Unable to decide whether to get in or get out, they push him into the crate and bury him with his mother.

Reality: Veronica's death and burial.

Helen's Story: Papa in Jail

Helen’s prison story anticipates Henry’s arrest and the children’s flight by boat. Her verse fails; she says Bagarthach often fails in a dream. [1968, pp. 29–30]

Reality: Foreshadows Henry's arrest and the children's departure on the Île de France.

Veronica's Characteristic Aorach

Referenced in Chapter 2, Veronica's signature story explains how she and Witchy were "twins" born eleven months apart:

Imagine an Earth doctor trying to tell a mistress of the Aorach about something as fundamental as that.
— Narrator on Veronica’s birth story [1968, p. 19]

The narrator sides with Veronica’s mastery against the doctor’s objection. [1968, pp. 18–19]

Continue to: Puca Nature →

Puca Nature

Biology, abilities, appearance, and the fatal curse of Earth Allergy.

◊
What Are the Puca?

The Pucas combine alien and fairy identities. Henry speculates about Neanderthals and describes off-Earth history; neither settles an origin. Earth Sickness weakens the adults, but it has no uniform timetable: Pandemonium John has worked his circuit for decades. [1968, pp. 20–21, 89, 91–92]

Appearance

The Dual Aspect

Puca can appear either human or goblin, and the Dulanty parents deliberately bred for both:

"Some of the children should look like children of this place, and some of them should look like the children back home."
[1968, p. 12]

Human-Appearing ("Like Angels")

  • Elizabeth: "The blackest hair and the whitest skin in the world." Beautiful as an Earth child.
  • Charles: Looks "like an angel."
  • Helen: Pretty, distinguishable only by gleaming eyes and ear-flicking.

Goblin-Appearing ("Like Real Pucas")

  • Peter: one of the goblin-appearing children. [1968, p. 12]
  • Dorothy: Goblin-appearing.
  • John: The funniest-looking of all.
  • Bad John: Translucent goblin.

The Sideways Glimpse

"Look at them straight, and you'd hardly notice a thing. But look at them sideways accidentally sometimes, just catching them in the corner of your eye, and they'd scare the liver out of you."
[1968, p. 12]

Even the human-appearing children reveal their true nature when glimpsed indirectly. The lawyer in Chapter 12 sees "a veritable gargoyle" in his peripheral vision.

The Green Eyes

All Puca have green eyes that glow in the dark, a recurring motif in the novel:

"Six little pair of goblin eyes glowing green in the dark; and a seventh older pair nictitated by death slumber to a fainter green. And opposed to them, only the defenseless World!"
[1968, p. 144]

The Death Mask

In death, even human-appearing Puca reveal their alien nature:

"Henry's shot face had become somewhat unhuman in repose, but not less than human. The Dulantys could manage to look like regular people, till they had to laugh, or die."
[1968, p. 127]

Abilities

Bagarthach (Magical Verse)

See Bagarthach Verses for full treatment. Puca can kill, summon, curse, and transform through rhymed verse.

Physical Superiority

It was, of course, a war of the Worlds.
— Narrator on Henry’s fight with Marshall [1968, p. 96]

Henry defeats Marshall in hand-to-hand combat despite Earth Allergy. Frank moves with supernatural speed to catch Crocker. The children display abilities beyond Earth children.

Telepathic Speech

The lawyer observes in Chapter 12:

They think out loud when they wish to do so, and vocal cords (if such they have) have nothing to do with it.
— The lawyer’s waking dream, as narrated [1968, p. 102]

Aquatic Ability

In Chapter 3, the children swim in ways impossible for humans:

  • Staying underwater for extended periods
  • Swimming "like eels"
  • Comfort in water matching their home world ("land and water inextricably mixed")

Instinctive Music

Puca can play any instrument instinctively, as demonstrated during the concert with Pandemonium John.

Earth Allergy

☠
The Fatal Curse

Earth Sickness affects body, judgment, and disposition. The narrator first says the children suffered it lightly and acquired immunity; Peter’s later passion complicates this, while Witchy assures them at the end that it will not catch them. The text distinguishes youthful disturbance from the adults’ fatal decline and gives no medical system. [1968, pp. 20, 69–71, 142]

Symptoms

  • Flushing and "hot eye" (resembles drunkenness)
  • Wavering gait
  • Progressive weakness
  • Listlessness and loss of will
  • Tainting with "Earth outlook"
  • Death

Victims

  • Veronica: Dies early in the novel's chronology
  • Frank: Appears drunk but is suffering Earth Allergy; killed before it could claim him
  • Henry: Weakened by Earth Allergy; allows arrest; killed before it could claim him
  • Witchy: Dies of Earth Allergy in Chapter 16
  • Pandemonium John: "Old and tired and racked with Earth Allergy" but still alive

Frank's Condition

He wavered in his walk like a drunk, and he had the flushed look and the hot eye of a drunk. But he was sober as a Rogers County judge. It was the Earth Allergy that had caught up with him and sent him along reeling and sick, that would kill him soon if something else didn’t do it first.
— Narrator on Frank [1968, p. 58]

Ghost Children

Puca children who die may persist as ghosts, as Bad John demonstrates:

  • Translucent (visible and see-through simultaneously)
  • Invisible/inaudible to most Earth people
  • Can pass through walls and unlock doors
  • Cannot write, though can make marks some people see
  • Doesn't eat
  • Can see other ghosts (and be punched by them)
  • Eventually departs ("gone for good")
"He's no more a ghost than you are. He's scaredest of all of us of ghosts because he can see them oftenest, and they can punch him like they can't do it to us. Bad John is just different because he died when he was a baby."
[1968, p. 103]

Puca and Indians

The Puca were told they would be "in rapport with the Indian population," but their information was "centuries out of date." Despite this, mutual recognition persists:

  • Men at the Lost Moon Bar recognize Pucas through grandmother stories. [1968, p. 117]
  • Phoebe Jane Lanyard can "be as goblin as they could"
  • The children find kinship at Misu Mound ("a mountainful of murdered Indians")
  • Indians and Puca share an expression "when they have just killed someone"

Puca and Dogs

"There is an ancient antipathy between Pucas and every sort of dogs, but especially the great hounds."
[1968, p. 115]

The narrator first states a broad antipathy between Pucas and dogs, especially hounds. Henry’s search for a farm then distinguishes indifferent, frightened, hostile, and relatively reasonable dogs. [1968, pp. 115, 121–122]

❧
Kobolds and the Underground

The narrator eventually distinguishes Pucas from goblins by saying that they look more like kobolds. The German folkloric term can name household or underground spirits. Its mining associations fit the strip pits and mound tunnels; the novel’s Puca history is its own invention. [1968, p. 69]

Continue to: Cosmology →

Cosmology

The Four Worlds, the Hive Ghost, Dragons' Seed, and the theological underpinnings of Lafferty's vision.

The Four Worlds

🌍
Earth as One of Four

Earth is called one of the Four Worlds, but the set is not exhaustively identified. Mercator, Astrobe, and Camiroi are named in other contexts; Pandemonium John also speaks of a dozen worlds. The home landscape imagined by the children mixes land and water. [1968, pp. 20–21, 40, 73, 87]

The Mission

The adult Dulantys were sent to Earth by Puca "instructors" as "picked young couples" with a dual mandate:

  1. Primary: "Achieve accord with Earth": integrate with humanity
  2. Further task: consider whether something could be done with Earth, an ambition whose implications become increasingly coercive. [1968, pp. 20–21]

The mission has failed to secure accord. The children inherit both the ambition to alter Earth and the unresolved question of how to deal with its inhabitants; the final charge does not specify a second mission. [1968, pp. 20–23, 141–144]

The Hive Ghost

🐝
Earth's Collective Consciousness

The Puca observe that Earth people operate with a collective intelligence they cannot understand:

"The Hive Ghost hovers over them invisible, and they feel it from one end of their communities to the other. We can handle Earth individuals as though they were furniture or stones, but we cannot handle the Hive Ghost that hangs over them."
[1968, p. 21]
— Frank Dulanty

Properties

  • Earth people act with "lightning instinct": faster than thought
  • They possess "unity and communication of the hive"
  • Frank describes a collective instinct that, to him, works faster than thought. [1968, p. 21]
  • Individual Earth people are manageable; the collective is not

This explains how Lost Haven instinctively rejects the Dulantys: the townspeople sense the difference even when they cannot articulate it. "We sense you here as they wouldn't sense you in a larger or busier place."

Dragons' Seed

🐉
"A Time Bomb in You"

Henry reveals to Marshall that the Puca have left something behind on Earth: "dragons' eggs" that have "hatched and are going now":

"You'll not become dominant here. We'll kill you off like the damned dragons you are."

"Yes, I begin to think that you will. But you won't win by it. We've laid dragons' eggs behind us. They're hatched and going now. You'll not know the young while they're growing. They are a time bomb in you."
[1968, p. 92]

Interpretations

  • Children and successors: Henry’s image suggests Puca continuance beyond the adults’ deaths. [1968, p. 92]
  • Metaphorical: Ideas, arts, or cultural influences that will transform Earth
  • The Children: The six Dulanty children themselves, released by Witchy's charge

Witchy's Release

In Chapter 16, Witchy explicitly names the children as Dragons' Seed:

"I break the egg! I turn you loose! Oh, my own Dragons' Seed!"
[1968, p. 144]

The Primitive Ethic vs. Earth Ethics

The "Peculiar and Remarkable" Earth Ethic

Witchy describes an Earth ethic (implicitly Christian) that the Puca find both admirable and impossible:

"There is on this world a most peculiar and remarkable ethic. The people of this world fail it by not taking it literally enough. Ourselves, if we try it, will fail it by taking it too literally."
[1968, p. 141]

She tells of a Puca cousin who followed it literally ("If your right hand offend you, hack it off") until "there was nothing left of him but the torso."

The Puca Primitive Ethic

"Ourselves, we live by a more primitive ethic. We do not deny that it is primitive, but it is the only ethic that the Giver has given us yet. We live that primitive ethic all the way. Be swift, and be sudden! That is our secret."
[1968, p. 141]

Witchy offers the primitive ethic as the Pucas’ received rule while acknowledging the demands of another ethic. Her permission to kill and her preference for control and alteration are morally difficult, and Frank’s undelivered appeal to gentleness runs against them. [1968, pp. 134–135, 141–144]

The Haunted Planet

Earth is consistently portrayed as a haunted, hostile place: "the meanest world in all the universes." The Aorach stories of Chapter 1 establish Earth as a place where:

  • Pictures come alive and kill
  • Hotels vanish and identities blur
  • The dead don't know they're dead
  • Ghost trains run beneath houses
  • Death cannot be escaped through promises

The Reefs of Earth

The novel's title comes from the Heroic Chantey in Chapter 14:

"Stranded Like a Fool, Dulanty—
On the Reefs of Earth—Untimely—"
[1968, p. 125]

Earth is a reef, a hidden danger that wrecks travelers. The Dulantys are stranded on it, dying of Earth Allergy, persecuted by the natives, unable to return home.

Puca Origins

The Neanderthal Theory

Henry hints that the Puca may have been Earth's original intelligent species:

"There is enmity between our flesh from the beginning. We fought before, in an ice cave a million years ago, either on Earth or off it. You're an almost-man."
[1968, p. 94]
— Marshall to Henry

Henry’s Neanderthal suggestion is speculative. Marshall’s account of an ancient fight in an ice cave expresses his sense of primordial enmity. [1968, pp. 91, 94]

The Museum Hoax

Henry’s museum prank places a deceased kinsman, labeled Puca Man, beyond the representation of Modern Man. The joke asserts a superior place in the evolutionary display. [1968, p. 91]

Catholic Elements

Lafferty’s work engages Catholic questions. In this novel the theological claims are made by particular speakers:

Luke's Gospel

Henry quotes Luke 22:53 before his arrest:

“But this is their hour,” said Henry, “and the power of darkness.”
— Henry [1968, p. 34]

The Giver

Witchy refers to "the Giver" as the source of the Puca's primitive ethic, a divine being who has given them a different moral law than Earth people received.

Apotheosis

Dorothy’s verse calls the proposed fiery deaths an Apotheosis. The grand word turns murder into mock glorification. [1968, p. 24]

Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum

The Heroic Chantey's final line, "Nothing about monsters except good," parallels the Latin maxim nil de mortuis nisi bonum ("nothing about the dead except good"). It asks that only good be said of the Dulantys as monsters.

The Final Image

"Six little pair of goblin eyes glowing green in the dark; and a seventh older pair nictitated by death slumber to a fainter green.

And opposed to them, only the defenseless World!"
[1968, p. 144]

The ending places six living children and their dying mother against the world. The comic reversal draws sympathy to the Dulantys while the threat of their violence stays in view. [1968, p. 144]

Continue to: Timeline →

Firm anchors and relative sequence. The novel moves between recollection, simultaneous action, and later consequences; it gives no eleven-day calendar.

Shortly after midnightHenry is arrested. Elizabeth hides the axe.pp. 33–34

✦Curse and Fulfillment

Helen’s curse on Crocker and Peter’s curse on Stutgard date from arrival, about six weeks before the family’s collapse. Henry’s curse on Marshall occurs much later, in prison.

[1968, pp. 15–16, 95, 135–138]

Death Log

Deaths, departures, and reported killings, with the narrative evidence for each. The register covers the principal cases.

Person or groupWhat happensEvidence and pages
Bad JohnDied in infancy before the main action; stays with the family and finally goes with Frank.Backstory and reported departure, not a second death: pp. 14, 103, 141.
VeronicaDies of Earth Allergy two days before Henry’s arrest.Narrated: pp. 22, 33.
Coalfactor StutgardKilled by Crocker with an axe before John arrives.Aftermath, Bad John’s witness, and axe evidence: pp. 31–32, 108.
Baxter Bushyhead, Little Sad Sam Jones, Harold HarvestmanCharles takes them into the woods; returns with real ears; Dorothy says he killed them.Strong converging evidence of offstage killings, including the narrator’s silencer disclosure: pp. 76–81, 106–107.
The old priestOverwhelmed by Henry’s confession; dies in the Old Priests’ Home a month later.The narrator explicitly assigns causation: pp. 73–74.
HenryMarshall shoots him three times; Crocker shoots him in the face and kills him.Directly narrated: pp. 126–127.
Thomas ButterfieldMarshall shoots him with the jailer’s handgun to remove a witness.Directly narrated: pp. 127–128.
FrankMarshall strikes him from behind with the rifle butt and rolls him into the bog.Directly narrated: pp. 135–136.
CrockerSinks when Frank loses the noose-rope after Marshall’s blow.Directly narrated, fulfilling Helen’s curse: pp. 135–136.
MarshallKilled by Phoebe Jane’s rifle shot; Charles believes his own shot killed him and rolls the body into the bog.Narrator distinguishes effective shot from Charles’s belief: pp. 136–138.
WitchyDies aboard the departing raft after her admonition and final joke. Elizabeth answers her.Narrated in the fading seventh pair of eyes: pp. 141–144.
✦Other Registers of Death

The inset tales include Albert, Silly Jimmy, William, Tom, Polly, and the hotel man. Misu Mound contains the dead of many periods; Helen’s estimate is thirty thousand. Crocker recalls a victim of his dogs and the earlier deaths of Matthew and Mark. Pandemonium’s wife and daughter belong to songs the narrator expressly calls literal accounts.

[1968, pp. 7–14, 66–69, 82–86, 100, 114–115, 131]
✦Failed Killings Are Still Attempts

The Stinkers survive the attempted drowning; Amada escapes; Fiddler dodges gunfire. Dorothy’s spell against the household is countered.

[1968, pp. 24–35, 41–50]

Themes

Readings of the novel’s violence, comedy, art, and damaged world.

✦The Two Plots

The children’s war and the adults’ persecution proceed in different registers, but their objects and agents connect them. The stolen axe becomes legal evidence. Crocker’s hired captors carry the pursuit into the children’s refuge. Fulbert’s signal brings Charles into the last hunt, while Phoebe supplies the shot Charles mistakes for his own.

[1968, pp. 31–39, 76–81, 103–110, 132–138]
✦The Business of Lost Haven

Marshall describes roughly a thousand relief checks in a town with roughly three hundred people: the dead, departed, and invented stay profitable. False crop histories and mined land support another stream of payments; land obtained for a dollar an acre adds to the scheme. Stutgard’s persecution and Marshall’s ambition thus have material interests as well as racial hatred behind them. The Dulantys’ own dubious business sales complicate any clean division between corrupt humans and economically innocent Pucas.

[1968, pp. 20, 94–95]
✦Violence and the Child’s Perspective

The children intend extermination and attempt particular killings. The Stinkers, Amada, and Fiddler escape through accidents, deception, and agility; Phoebe’s hospitality creates a different obstacle. The offstage fate of the blackbirders is especially grave: real ears, a real silencer, and Dorothy’s complete accusation weigh against a sentimental reading.

Veronica dies of Earth Allergy, not at human hands. Human persecution is real, but the novel does not endorse extermination as the answer to it. The narration’s participation in the children’s perspective is itself part of the moral problem.

[1968, pp. 22, 24–32, 41–50, 79–81, 106]
✦Frank’s Unspoken Counsel and Witchy’s Charge

Frank intends to tell the children to deal gently with the world and seek a broader way. His murder prevents the speech. Witchy’s delivered admonition permits killing yet shifts their immediate purpose from killing everybody to controlling and altering. Her thought about responsibility escapes her. Together the two counsels leave an ethical argument unfinished.

[1968, pp. 134–135, 141–144]
✦Indigenous Alliance and Puca Ambition

Phoebe Jane, John Loose Screw, Sammy Bluefield, and the dead of the mound offer forms of recognition denied by Lost Haven’s rulers. This affinity is not identity. The Puca have their own projects of dominance and speak of becoming an elite; their original mission is not established as flight from an expulsion at home. Witchy is an institutionalized adult, while removal of the children is still only a threatened action. These differences bear on the colonial analogy.

[1968, pp. 20–21, 26–28, 34, 66–69, 92, 117]
✦Art, Refuge, and the Damaged Landscape

The strip pits are industrial wreckage and a child’s terrain of invention, an image of home and a battlefield. Misu Mound provides refuge among the dead while preserving competing stories and deep layers of burial. The honkeroo makes artistic joy inseparable from monstrous lyrics. An Oklahoma Gothic reading sits beside a pastoral one, concerned with what home, art, and freedom can be made in a damaged place.

[1968, pp. 40, 66–70, 82–90, 100, 132–133]
✦Faith, Literalism, and the Anointed

Henry’s theology differs from the priest’s despite his scriptural learning. He approaches the Bible as Earth mythology and says the Puca do not generally believe the Anointed has yet been born. The priest asks whether salvation reaches intelligent aliens. Witchy’s literal reading of Christian commands, her appeal to a primitive ethic, and her fading responsibility keep the theological difficulty open. Dorothy’s word Apotheosis makes a murderous joke.

[1968, pp. 24, 71–74, 141–144]
✦Story, Satire, and Authority

Aorach includes more than ghost tales. Veronica’s birth story defeats the doctor’s objection in the narrator’s telling; Pandemonium’s family songs are called literal. Yet Helen’s inventions are challenged, Phoebe’s Puca burial layer is rejected, and professors’ certainty is mocked. The novel tests who can tell the truth and what a literal account can contain.

[1968, pp. 18–19, 51–54, 67–68, 85–86]
✦Fairy Terror and the Final Reversal

Irish Pooka tradition already includes frightening and coercive encounters. His Pucas add extraterrestrial history, illness, art, and family loyalties to that difficult inheritance. The final defenseless World is a comic reversal of power whose promise and threat stay together. The four ABAB quatrains of chapter titles announce the move toward alteration; the book ends before the children’s later rule can be judged.

[1968, pp. 7–14, 139–144]

For the folklore comparison, see the Dúchas records in Sources & Editorial Notes.

❧
Allusion as Part of the Action

Borrowed language repeatedly becomes an instrument or a difficulty within the plot. Peter turns Laocoon’s warning into a prediction about the murder weapon. Marshall uses Gogol to explain profitable fraud, then treats literary knowledge as a possession that should give him mastery. Henry answers with a verse whose promised rifle will fire after his death. Scripture is quoted, altered, falsely attributed, argued over, and taken disastrously literally. The references do work in the story. [1968, pp. 15–16, 34, 64–65, 71–74, 94–95, 137, 141–144]

Sources: Virgil, Aeneid 2.49; Gogol, Dead Souls, part 1, ch. 11.

Glossary

Key terms, Puca vocabulary, regional language, and specialized concepts.

Puca Terms

Aorach (possibly from Irish aoire or aerach)

Puca narrative art, broader than ghost stories. Irish aorach means satirical; aerach is a distinct word. See Aorach Stories. [1968, pp. 18–19]

Bagarthach (possibly from Irish bagairt, "threat")

Puca verse with power to act on bodies and events. Irish bagarthach is a form referred to bagrach, threatening. The novel shows counterverses and disputed limits. See Bagarthach Verses. [1968, pp. 18–19, 35]

Dragons' Seed

What Witchy calls the children when releasing them in Chapter 16. Also refers to "dragons' eggs" Henry mentions, meaning Puca influences left on Earth as "a time bomb in you." See Cosmology.

Earth Allergy

The illness of Pucas on Earth. Early statements of the children’s immunity coexist with Peter’s later distress and Witchy’s final reassurance. The adults’ decline has no fixed timetable. See Puca Nature. [1968, pp. 20, 69–71, 89, 142]

Four Worlds, The

Earth is one of four, but the four are not securely enumerated. Other passages name Mercator, Astrobe, and Camiroi and mention a dozen worlds. [1968, pp. 20–21, 73, 87]

Hive Ghost

The Puca term for Earth's collective human consciousness. "The Hive Ghost hovers over them invisible... We can handle Earth individuals as though they were furniture or stones, but we cannot handle the Hive Ghost that hangs over them." See Cosmology.

Kindred

Other Pucas. Frank invokes Kindred while explaining the counterverse that defeated Dorothy’s spell. An inset tale complicates a universal claim of immunity. [1968, pp. 8–9, 35]

Primitive Ethic

The moral code the Puca follow, distinct from Earth's "peculiar and remarkable ethic" (Christianity). "We live by a more primitive ethic... Be swift, and be sudden! That is our secret."

Puca (from Irish púca)

The alien/fairy species to which the Dulantys belong. Can appear human or goblin. Possess magical abilities through Bagarthach. In Irish folklore, the púca is a shape-shifting creature associated with harvest time and trickery.

Puca Sleep Hold

A technique for rendering someone unconscious. Henry uses it on the jailer during his escape: "He throttled the jailer very gently and stretched him out to sleep on the floor."

The Giver

Witchy's term for the divine being who gave the Puca their primitive ethic. "The only ethic that the Giver has given us yet."

Locations & Geography

Big Shanty, The

The Dulanty home in Lost Haven, a large structure built over old railroad tracks, rented from an Indian lady in Catoosa. See Lost Haven.

Catoosa

A town in Rogers County, Oklahoma, near Lost Haven. The Indian lady who owns the Big Shanty lives here. Butterfield's farm is "near Catoosa."

Five Kingdoms, The

The strip pit territories conquered or allied by the Dulanty children: Stinkers, Stutgard Landing, Fiddler's Landing, Lanyard Landing, and Faber Stronghold. See The Strip Pits.

Green River

The main waterway threading through the strip pits. The children spend their "first night at sea" moored here.

Lost Haven

The shabby, overgrown Oklahoma town where the Dulantys live for six weeks. Its corrupt economic order is disclosed by Marshall. [1968, pp. 15, 94–95]

Lost Moon Bar

The bar where Indigenous men recognize and help Henry during his escape. [1968, pp. 116–120]

Misu Mound

Burial mound with contested histories. Helen estimates thirty thousand dead. The children find kinship there; Helen later exchanges a buffalo thighbone for a dead woman’s own bone. [1968, pp. 66–69, 100, 132–133]

Strip Pits

"A dozen square miles of mountains turned inside out, threaded by canals, and with bottomless chasms." The remnants of surface coal mining, now the children's domain. See The Strip Pits.

Vessels

Île de France (French: "Island of France")

Fulbert’s fishing raft, deeded to the children for whisky. Its grand name suits his royal pretensions; a specific ocean-liner allusion is possible but unconfirmed. [1968, pp. 35–39]

Sea Bear

The Stinkers' raft, captured during the Battle of Port Stinker. Towed behind the Île de France.

Characters & Nicknames

Ange-Jacques (French: "Angel James/Jacques")

Fulbert Fronsac's name for Bad John. One of the few people who can see and hear the ghost child.

Bad John

The ghost child, John's brother who died as an infant but persists with the family. "If you count him," there are seven children. See Bad John.

Catherine de Medici

Fulbert’s she-goat. The narrator gives her royal ancestry in the tall-tale register. The deed grants her guest status on the raft. [1968, pp. 36–38]

Crocker's Crocks

The men who follow Crocker's orders in the lynch mob.

Lost Dauphin, The

Fulbert is the lost Dauphin, or his son or grandson, with the identity shifting in the telling. [1968, p. 35]

Pandemonium

John’s wheeled musical apparatus. Forty or fifty instruments describes the smaller seagoing version proposed for Charles. [1968, pp. 88–89]

Witchy

The mother's Earth name (her Puca name is Briochtog). Called "Witchy" for her unearthly beauty and manner.

Regional & Historical Terms

Choc Beer

Oklahoma homemade beer, made in varied ways. Tobacco appears in one historical report; production and consumption were not exclusively Choctaw. See the Oklahoma Historical Society source. [1968, pp. 45–46]

Corbie (Scots)

A crow or raven. Used in Helen's crow-summoning Bagarthach: "I sing the corbie to the corb!"

Greek Fire

Helen's improvised incendiary weapons: burning paper sacks filled with glass, thumbtacks, cockleburs, and cactus. Named after the Byzantine naval weapon.

Outre Scene (French: "excessive, extravagant")

The climactic scene in Puca drama where "all the bloody stuff is heaped together for the greater enjoyment and convenience of all." Chapter 15 is the novel's outre scene.

Rogers County

A county in northeastern Oklahoma where Lost Haven is located. Real place; Lafferty lived in nearby Tulsa.

T-Town

Tulsa, Oklahoma. The lawyer Fulbert brings is from "T-Town."

Latin Phrases

De Profundis in Patinam

"From the depths into the dish" is a fragment from the Heroic Chantey (Chapter 14). Parodies De Profundis (Psalm 130, "Out of the depths I cry to you").

Nil de Monstris Nisi Bonum

"Nothing about monsters except good" is the final line of the Heroic Chantey. Parodies nil de mortuis nisi bonum ("nothing about the dead except good").
